subtopic: MR. KNOWLES  SUGGESTED MEETING OF PARTY LEADERS WITH PROCEDURE SUBCOMMITTEE

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: MR. KNOWLES  SUGGESTED MEETING OF PARTY LEADERS WITH PROCEDURE SUBCOMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. Although I have not indicated to you, sir, or to anyone else the point of privilege which I wish to raise, I am sure it will be clear in a moment that it is a matter of concern to the entire house.
On August 12, entirely on my own, I addressed an open letter to the leaders of the parties in the House of Commons in which I suggested that consideration might be given to ways and means of arranging in the future to avoid unnecessarily protracted debate. My letter had nothing to do with the current debate on the flag. It looked only to the future, and it was based on the proposition of acting only by agreement amongst all parties.
I am happy to report, Mr. Speaker, that I have now had a reply by letter from each of the party leaders. One of the letters is marked "Personal" and I shall therefore not disclose its contents. Indeed, I shall not make public any of the letters unless I am authorized to do so. I feel I can say to the house, however, and I am sure the house will be happy to hear this, that there is a wide measure of agreement amongst the five party leaders in their replies. Some of the letters seemed to agree with what I set out in my letter, although all of them did not go that far. However, all the leaders are united in their desire to do everything they can to improve the procedures of this House of Commons.
In view of this, Mr. Speaker-and this is my point of privilege-I should like to suggest that there should be a meeting of the five party leaders with the members of the subcommittee on procedure, which is a subcommittee of Your Honour's committee on procedure and organization. I suggest that there be such a meeting, not for the purpose of discussing the current flag debate but rather for the purpose of looking to the
future to achieve what all the leaders have expressed, the desire to improve the procedures of this House of Commons.
I therefore wish to suggest that if within the next day or two the five leaders would indicate to me, as chairman of the subcommittee, their willingness to attend such a meeting I would call a meeting of that subcommittee for the purpose of extending an invitation to them. I realize, Mr. Speaker, that one should consider that this suggestion is being addressed to the party leaders, and a case could be made for their holding a meeting on their own, but I am sure members realize that this is a matter of concern to the House of Commons as a whole, and that it would be proper for such a meeting to be held by the subcommittee on procedure, to be attended by the five party leaders for the purpose of having this discussion. I should like to go one step further and suggest that at such a meeting, Your Honour might also be present. If you are willing to do so, you might also make your chambers or some other room available for the holding of such a meeting.
I hope consideration will be given to such a proposition, and I express to the house my pleasure at the replies I have received from the five party leaders.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: MR. KNOWLES  SUGGESTED MEETING OF PARTY LEADERS WITH PROCEDURE SUBCOMMITTEE
speechtext:
I begin by asking Your Honour whether this is a question of privilege. It seems to me like a specious endeavour to raise a question of privilege and designate it as such when, in fact, it is not.
Then there was a reference to a personal letter. I was rather surprised that the hon. gentleman should have found that the best means of communicating his views was through the instrumentality of an open letter to the press. Be that as it may, it was most unusual. I thought it could have been raised in the house or through the ordinary means of communication by post. This procedure was not followed by the hon. gentleman.
He mentioned a personal letter. I think the one I wrote to him was personal, but I will be only too pleased to have it published. In so far as the suggested meeting is concerned, however, the committee has its

Inquiries of the Ministry representatives from the various parties. Let the committee on procedure continue its work. It has done very good work. Certainly to bring up such a matter in the manner in which the hon. gentleman has just brought this before the house does not indicate that degree of care that should characterize the handling of questions like this. If he had brought it to one's attention outside the house or through any other means of communication, it could be understood. I simply say that our desire has always been to expedite the business of the house within the limitation that we discharge our constitutional responsibility.

subtopic: MR. KNOWLES  SUGGESTED MEETING OF PARTY LEADERS WITH PROCEDURE SUBCOMMITTEE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: MR. KNOWLES  SUGGESTED MEETING OF PARTY LEADERS WITH PROCEDURE SUBCOMMITTEE
speechtext: I immediately say to the hon. gentleman that having secured the publicity he apparently desired, I will be only too happy to have publication of my letter, which he can release immediately if he chooses.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. KNOWLES  SUGGESTED MEETING OF PARTY LEADERS WITH PROCEDURE SUBCOMMITTEE
speechtext: For our guidance in the future will Your Honour declare whether this was a valid point of privilege?

subtopic: MR. KNOWLES  SUGGESTED MEETING OF PARTY LEADERS WITH PROCEDURE SUBCOMMITTEE
speechtext: I think it is clear that one cannot determine whether a question is one of privilege until you hear what it is. Usually, to be effective, it seems to me a question of privilege should conclude with some sort of motion asking the house to do something, or asking that a decision be reached. There was no conclusion to this projected question of privilege, and in the circumstances I can only say it is quite unusual. I want to assure the house that the Chair, of course, knew nothing about this, but that is beside the point. Perhaps some useful service was rendered by the hon. member rising at this time, but may I suggest that we get on with our business.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. KNOWLES  SUGGESTED MEETING OF PARTY LEADERS WITH PROCEDURE SUBCOMMITTEE
speechtext: A flagrant abuse of the rules; that is what it was.

speakeroldname: Hon. G. J. Mcllrailh (President of the Privy Council):
maintopic: PUBLIC SERVICE PROTESTS RESPECTING RECENT SALARY INCREASES
speechtext:
On Friday last, as appears on page 7114 of Hansard, in response to a question from the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, and again yesterday, as reported on page 7168, in reply to the Leader of the Opposition, the Prime Minister promised to review with me the representations that have been received from the civil service organizations with respect to the recently announced group B salary revisions.
This is to report that we have reviewed this matter and, in doing so, have paid particular attention to the rates for grades 1 and 2 typists, clerks and stenographers in whose positions both hon. members expressed a special interest.
Inquiries of the Ministry
We are satisfied, after further examination of the problem and from the careful study which has been given to the whole range of group B salary rates by the ministers on the treasury board, that the rates which have been announced are fair and equitable, and place the government's salary levels on a basis which compares favourably with other employers in Canada. There are numerous comparisons which could be made, including comparisons based upon data derived from the pay research bureau surveys, to confirm what I have said. However, pay research bureau reports are confidential, and I am therefore obliged to make the following comparison on the basis of data available from public sources.
To illustrate my point, we have compared the rates now announced for typists, clerks and stenographers 1 and 2 with the rates in force under collective bargaining agreements between the Saskatchewan government employees association and the government of that province. In five of the six classes referred to the maximum rate now effective in the federal service is equal to or greater than the maximum provided under collective agreements in the Saskatchewan service.
I should also say a word, I think, with reference to the claim that large numbers of the employees in group B have not received a salary increase in four years. This is not in fact correct. The ranges of pay for typists, clerks and stenographers grade 1 all contain at least seven steps, and while rates of pay may remain unchanged for a period of time, employees entering these classes are entitled to semi-annual statutory increases of $90 a year until they reach the maximum. For group B as a whole the increase in the actual levels of pay over the two year period since the last review amounts to approximately 6.4 per cent and this latest increase in the rates of pay will add another 3.4 per cent to this increase, making an increase in the actual salary level of the order of about 10 per cent over the two year period.
As for the question asked by the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue on Friday last as reported in Hansard on page 7114 regarding the position of the corresponding classes on the House of Commons staff, while I may point out that this matter is under the jurisdiction and responsibility of Your Honour perhaps I could have the indulgence of the house to say that prior to the question being asked last Friday, action had already been initiated to deal with the revision of the salary rates for this group. This is in

Inquiries of the Ministry accordance with the usual procedures tor reviewing the salary rates of the clerical, stenographic and other office classes of the House of Commons staff concurrently with the group B.
As I have indicated, since this matter is in your hands, Mr. Speaker, and while it is not perhaps entirely appropriate for me to say when the announcement of the revision will be made, may I be permitted to indicate that I expect it will be made very soon.

The Prime Minister has indicated that he is prepared to submit this matter to a committee as long as a time limit is placed on its deliberations as well as on the debates in this house when the question is brought back to the Commons. This seems to be a further indication of his intention to use his authority to force Canadians to accept his three maple leaf design.
I think there is no necessity for a time limit to be placed on the work of the committee. Surely such a committee should be given all the time it needs in order to reach a conclusion. My own belief is that such a committee could reach agreement. After all, the committee set up in 1945 was virtually unanimous in the conclusion it reached. I think another committee could reach a similar measure of agreement provided no time limit were placed on its work, and if its members began their task with a real intention to do something about this controversial question which has upset the nation so much, even if compromises were necessary in order to achieve this purpose.
Perhaps the first question which should be placed on any plebiscite is, do Canadians really want a new flag? This is a question I have encountered from time to time, and it is a question I have often asked myself. If it were put to a plebiscite, this house would know the feeling of Canadians generally in this regard. If the answers showed that Canadians do want a new flag, then we could set ourselves to work in an effort to evolve, or find, that new flag, one which would be satisfactory to the majority of the people and which would unite our country rather than divide it.
Everything has its good points, even this flag debate. The debate has made Canadians more aware of the Canadian flag, more aware of the red ensign than ever before. A few months ago I was shocked at the number of Canadians who were asking what is on the red ensign, and what does it mean, anyway?
I think this unawareness stems from the lack of teaching in schools across Canada, particularly on the subject of Canadian history. Canadians are more ignorant about Canadian history than they are about the

history of the United States or Britain. One could ask any number of school children about the war of 1812, and I imagine that not more than one out of 100 could say very much about it. I think ignorance of the red ensign, the Canadian flag, stems from the fact that very little Canadian history is taught in our schools across Canada. If better instruction were given we should all be very much more aware of the history of the red ensign, because this flag certainly has close links with Canada's past.
In 1945, under the order in council passed on September 5, the government of that day set out clearly that the red ensign, as modified, was Canada's distinctive flag to be used wherever a distinctive flag for Canada might be needed. This was generally accepted at the time. The question which arises in my mind is, why this sudden need for a reappraisal of the whole flag question in 1964? The Prime Minister suggested, in a television talk I believe, that it came about because he had promised a new flag. Well, the Minister of Transport at one time promised two flags and, indeed, three flags for Canada.
We all want to see a united Canada. We want to see one flag for all Canada; this is the only way in which Canada will remain united. To return to this question of the need for a reappraisal of the flag situation in 1964, the Prime Minister, it is said, promised a new flag for 1965.
He promised other things, too.

He promised a lot of other things, too. A promise was made about milk, and we discussed that promise this afternoon. The Minister of Agriculture told all Canadians we would have a school milk program. Now we have a surplus of milk in Alberta and he says he cannot touch the problem. Another promise which we in western Canada remember very well is the promise with regard to $2 wheat. We have not seen it and we are unlikely to see it fulfilled by 1965 or even by 1968. We could talk about the time the minister of northern affairs made a number of promises. That was before he became a member of the cabinet. This promise about the flag could be regarded in the same light. It was made before the hon. member for Algoma East (Mr. Pearson) became Prime Minister.
People can only form their opinions in the light of their own knowledge, I suppose, but I do know that the new flag was never waved about in western Canada in 1963. It was never proclaimed that this promise was one
Canadian Flag
the Liberals intended to keep. It was certainly not proclaimed as loudly or as often as the promise about $2 wheat. As a matter of fact, in my constituency I heard no talk whatsoever about the introduction of a new flag; neither did anything on this subject appear in the weekly newspapers. The hon. member for York-Humber made this position very clear when he spoke yesterday. He told us the flag was not promised in Toronto.
So where was it promised, and for what purpose? I do not wish to contribute to any division which already exists in this country, but we know that the promise of a new flag served the Prime Minister well. Why did he bring it before this parliament? It was not mentioned in the speech from the throne. I suggest the Prime Minister brought it forward because he had very little other legislation ready. He is using this flag debate as a filler. He tells us "Pass the flag resolution and we will give you a recess". This will give them more time to prepare their pension legislation, more time to discuss things of that nature with the provinces. The Prime Minister has promised the house many things; in particular, a recess if we accept this flag. I said yesterday that I am proud to be a member of a party that puts duty before holidays.
Hear, hear.

The Prime Minister has clearly brought Canada's flag into the political arena. For what purpose, he knows best; but I think it should certainly be taken out of the political arena, because we want Canadians all across this country to accept the flag once it is chosen. We are well able to gather that the flag at present proposed by the Prime Minister is not acceptable to many Canadians. Therefore it must be referred to a standing committee which can study the whole subject at great length.
I noticed an editorial in the Quebec Chronicle of August 8 which I think is very significant to this particular debate. It says in part:
For reasons he knows best, Mr. Pearson has made a political issue of the flag: and he could not have picked on a worse time. Introduced in rather authoritarian fashion in the house, with no popular consultation and in the teeth of fierce opposition from a large section of the public, the flag question, far from settling anything, has only stirred unnecessary controversy and a great deal of recrimination.
Mr. Pearson surely knew (there were plenty of public statements which pointed to it) that any flag, as long as it did not contain references to the histories of either of the two founding nations, would be acceptable to the French Canadians. Why then did he not consult the people

Canadian Flag
on a design which would have been universally acceptable? One Liberal answer to this is that it would not have been practical.
I think that is a very weak answer indeed. This editorial goes on to say:
But this is utter nonsense. All legislation is, in fact, based on the principle of popular consultation. Why else do we go through the enormously costly motions of electing a new government every four years? Why else do we give our M.P.'s the right to speak for us?
It goes on to deal at great length with some of the problems this flag has run into because of the time at which the Prime Minister chose to present it to parliament. I will not read the rest of this editorial, Mr. Speaker, but I believe it deals with the question very well. It states that the Prime Minister has brought this flag into the political arena at the worst possible time, when the country is divided enough, without adding to the problem. Certainly it has already been proven that this flag issue is adding to that division.
In looking at the four questions contained in the subamendment one notices that the first question suggested by the hon. member for Regina City is "Are you in favour of the Canadian red ensign?" I think I should point out that in going back over the history of the red ensign we find it was flown by the Hudson's Bay Company. This trading company was more or less the founder of western Canada, particularly, and most of eastern Canada. They used the red ensign as their flag and the flag of Canada. I might point out, Mr. Speaker, that this company were perhaps more than just a trading company. They were the government of the day; they had powers far more sweeping than many governments; they could arm ships, punish offenders, enforce laws, and so on. In fact they controlled the whole area that is now western Canada; and at that time, away back in the early 1800's, the Hudson's Bay Company used the red ensign as their flag.
Coming to a later period, in 1841 northern Manitoba used this flag. It flew over Fort Garry at the junction of the Red and Assini-boine rivers. Hon. members have referred to the fact that in 1904 and 1905 the red ensign was flown as the flag of Canada. In 1922 an order in council was passed authorizing the use of the new Canadian coat of arms on the fly of the red ensign.
Mr. Speaker, may I ask the hon. member a question?
Certainly.

I understand the hon. member said the Hudson's Bay Company had used- I forget the date-the red ensign as its flag.

Has the Hudson's Bay Company, however, changed that practice? Do they still not use it as their flag?

Being a very loyal company, Mr. Speaker, I suggest that perhaps they do. In 1924 a government order in council authorized the use of the red ensign on all Canadian government buildings in foreign countries. In 1934 the Bennett government declared the red ensign to be our national colours. During the second world war the King government chose the red ensign as the flag for the commander of the Canadian army overseas. Mackenzie King has often been quoted in this house, Mr. Speaker, and perhaps I may be allowed to quote him once more with regard to the Canadian flag. Mr. King said this:
The red ensign, with the Canadian coat of arms in the fly has, for over 70 years been very generally used in situations where a flag specially distinctive of Canada was essential. It was first authorized by the government of Sir John A. Macdonald shortly after confederation for use on Canadian merchant vessels. It has been popularly accepted as a flag distinctive of Canada.
Certainly the red ensign flew over the houses of commons of Upper and Lower Canada at the time of confederation. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, if one looks back over Canadian history one can see that as history unfolded the red ensign was there. This parliament has defended the flag many times. During one attack back in 1949 Mr. King said this:
Canadians have fought and died under this flag. The red ensign should be good enough for anyone.
Hear, hear.

Every prospective immigrant is informed what our flag is by the Department of Citizenship and Immigration. They are advised that the flag used as distinctive of Canada is properly described as the Canadian red ensign, with the shield of the coat of arms in the fly. This should point out to most members that the red ensign has very strong claims indeed to being called Canada's distinctive flag, and certainly the first question submitted by the hon. member for Regina City has a right to that place.
In view of the great deal of controversy over the flag question the hon. member has referred to a modified form of the red ensign in question No. 2, perhaps one which would set out more clearly the two founding races of this great country of ours. Certainly this has merit, because if it can bring greater unity to this divided country in which we now

find ourselves, it will be very worth while. Anything that can bring greater unity to this country should be seriously considered. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I would wholeheartedly support the second question, if such a flag were favoured by most Canadians as the result of a plebiscite being held.
The third question contained in the hon. member's subamendment is, "Are you in favour of a three maple leaf design?" One wonders why one should be in favour of such a design. Naturally, being an agriculturist, when the suggested Pearson pennant was brought forward I looked at the maple trees in Ontario and even those in Quebec to see if three maple leaves grew naturally, as suggested by the Pearson pennant or the Pearson flag, as it is now called. I failed to find any resemblance whatsoever. I immediately wondered, why three; why not five? It seemed to me maple leaves grew in clusters of five more frequently than in any other number; I never found them growing in threes. Why not one maple leaf, as has been suggested by the New Democratic party? Certainly the timing of this flag resolution has been poor; the advance notice on behalf of the government has been poor, and the authoritative manner in which the government has presented its three maple leaf design has been poor.
I could not help noticing an article which appeared in the Ottawa Citizen of August 22 from Southam news services, written by that noted reporter Charles Lynch. Mr. Lynch states in this article:
To me, Mr. Pearson's decisiveness introducing the three leaf flag, as a focal point around which new flag sentiment could rally, was admirable. In decisive fashion, he made it clear that this was the new flag and that the government would stand or fall on it. Now was the time for all good Canadians to rally 'round.
But in the next breath he trotted out the union jack, to be endorsed for Canadians as our symbol of Queen and commonwealth. This preposterous proposal started the erosion of his position, arrested only momentarily by the action of Mr. Speaker Macnaughton who broke the leaves and the jack into two separate resolutions.
In the subsequent confusion, the Prime Minister seemed to be saying that he would stake the life of his government on adoption of the union jack, in its Queen and commonwealth context.
Now he has made it clear that he isn't staking the life of his government on any flag-leaves, jacks, or what have you.
And instead of fighting valiantly for the three leaf flag that he unveiled so dramatically last spring, he's saying that he'll agree to referral of the flag matter to a parliamentary committee, provided a time limit is set both on the committee's work and on the subsequent debate in parliament on whatever the committee recommends.
Canadian Flag
This seems to me to be a considerable retreat from his previous position of solid support for the three leaf flag.
And if the Prime Minister is retreating from the three leaf flag, the three leaf flag would appear to have little chance of ever being run up the parliamentary flagpole.
Mr. Lynch then says:
What weakened Mr. Pearson's position?
Mr. Lynch then suggests reasons for this weakened position. Mr. Speaker, perhaps you will bear with me while I read another portion of this article. Mr. Lynch states:
One factor has been his own unwillingness, and that of his Liberal colleagues, to stump the country in support of the three leaf flag.
In other words he is suggesting there is some dissension among Liberal backbenchers, and Mr. Pearson is just a little bit confused as to whether he would have the support of his party after the members got out on the election hustings, away from parliament and out from under his thumb. He is suggesting that perhaps these backbenchers when fighting in their own ridings would not be proud to fly the three maple leaf flag, and it would not receive the unanimous endorsation that Mr. Pearson thought it might.
Mr. Lynch then states in the last paragraph of this article under the heading "The Red Ensign is Now Stronger Than Ever":
If not above the battle, it at least flew over the battlefield-
He was referring to the House of Commons.
-and its position seems considerably stronger at summer's end than it was at the beginning.
Mr. Pearson is ready to throw the design of a a new flag back into committee-a far cry from hopes that it would be flying by July 1, or for the royal visit in October.
Mr. Lynch is suggesting that the government is going to withdraw its flag and refer it to a committee in the hope that the committee can bring the government out of its state of confusion, and out of this hopeless situation it has brought parliament to, without losing too much face. Mr. Lynch then commends to opposition party for standing up for what it thought was right, in an effective debate in respect of this flag issue.
Certainly I should like to see this flag issue resolved. I know my constituents would like to see this house get on with the more urgent business of parliament, including the pension legislation, legislation in respect of the railways, which is of great concern to western Canada, legislation in respect of the Hall report, also of vital concern to Canadians, to say nothing of the legislation promised by the Minister of Agriculture six or seven

Canadian Flag
months ago, which he said will revolutionize agriculture in Canada it only the opposition will allow him to bring it in. I am sure we are all agreeable to allowing him to bring in this legislation. I invite him to do so, and we will deal with it.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I must advise the hon. member that the time allowed him has expired.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak on the subamendment now before this house, because I feel that for several reasons I am in almost a unique position.
Those of us who live in the Northwest Territories have real difficulty in masking our incredulity and containing our amusement at the prospect of you sophisticated southerners trying to suffocate each other with an issue which on the surface at least has little real significance to us in the north. It is perhaps this very sort of thing that motivates some Canadians to move into the Northwest Territories, where there is enough work to do each day to keep their minds off these interesting but hardly productive problems.
For my own part, I do not have any mandate from my constituents on this particular issue. I believe I have received altogether four letters in the past year, three of them asking that the red ensign be retained and one asking that the new flag be a single maple leaf design. In fact only one person suggested anything, should there be a necessity to change the flag and after all, 10,000 of my constituents live in the Canadian barren lands.
I should like to ask you this question, Mr. Speaker. Have you ever tried to explain three maple leaves to an Eskimo who has never seen a tree? I ask you, Mr. Speaker, would you like to fight an election about a flag, going to voters who have no access to flagpoles? What in God's name, we in the territories ask, is all this about? Who decided that now was the time to proceed with this issue? The people of the north on my recent visit continually asked me, what is going on? I could only tell them that our Prime Minister has chosen a design for a new flag and has said that until it is accepted the other business of parliament must remain on the shelf. I have told them that, if he chose, the Prime Minister could bring forward other pieces of legislation that are of direct concern to them, such as the pension plan, legislation in respect of the Hall commission report, and even legislation, which is

long overdue in the Northwest Territories, giving the people of the north the right to vote in territorial elections. But in the eyes of the Prime Minister the right to vote takes second place to three maple leaves waving proudly over their heads on metal flagpoles.
What else can I say to answer the question of what is happening in this place, when asked by people who need schools, roads, hospitals and jobs to give them even half a chance to raise their families in health and decency? This prime ministerial preoccupation with a new flag is incomprehensible. To me personally, but speaking as a northern Canadian, the whole business is a pathetically stupid piece of fumbling by a Prime Minister devoted to tokenism in the handling of Canadian domestic problems. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that the conversion of the flag debate in a barely disguised underground battle between the two founding races is a direct result of the ineptitude of the Prime Minister and more particularly of his advisers. The issue is not a real one, nor is the proposed solution a real solution. The subamendment we have before us is, as I see it, an attempt to modify and change a basically unsound and unfortunate government resolution.
I have spoken about these matters before and I intend to do so again today. When we talk about tokenism surely the parallel is obvious, that parallel being the B and B commission. This, after all, was one of the greatest exercises in tokenism that any Canadian prime minister has ever attempted. This is saying to people who have legitimate complaints, who have legitimate feelings of injustice on certain matters, "We will give you a commission where the extremists among you can run off at the mouth. It will change nothing really but we will say in the next election, see what we have done, we have set up the B and B commission," as though that accomplished anything.
This is what the flag issue is, too, because the Prime Minister and the government will go to the people of the country and say, see here are three maple leaves; you have unity, you have a nation. This is nonsense, and it is the most vicious kind of nonsense that could be perpetrated on the Canadian people at this time. I say it is vicious because I believe this issue is postponing in fact two essential steps that have to be taken to achieve Canadian unity. As I see them, these two steps are in the first place the repatriation of the constitution, which we know is being worked on but which will be postponed in the

artificial atmosphere of a new flag; and second, a hard headed review of the responsibilities and the revenues in each of the federal and provincial spheres of government.
This is the work that needs to be done to give Canada a new sense of national purpose. What frightens me about the flag is that should it be accepted, be it three maple leaves or one, be they red or green, it will be used to say to the people, "Here, you really have something," when in fact the basic problems confronting this nation will have been postponed for an even longer period.
I suggest to the Prime Minister that if he wants to meet the needs of certain areas of Canada he should state firmly now the position his government will take in relation to new kinds of revenue and new kinds of arrangements that will be made with the provinces. Quebec has legitimate demands that must be met. What I want the Prime Minister to do is to outline these views to the house and the country, and say to Quebec and all the other provinces, "Beyond this we do not go".
I say that because what is bothering many people is a vague feeling of unease that there is no end to the demands that will be made by a group of people in a minority position who feel, perhaps quite rightly, that they have been treated unjustly. Such action on the part of the Prime Minister would do much in itself to remove the malaise that is affecting many Canadians and that causes them to interpret every act of the government as some kind of appeasement to Quebec, whether it is or not.
At this point I want to take a few moments to register strong objection to the efforts of numerous members of parliament from the province of Quebec in all parties to appoint themselves as the sole spokesmen for the so-called French Canadian people. I am a French Canadian from the Northwest Territories. I am as French Canadian as anyone in the House of Commons. I can trace my ancestry back to 1665 and an early deserter from the French forces. I am able to read French and can speak it haltingly, sufficiently well to get by. Indeed, I am relearning the language, and within a year I should be able to chatter along with the best of you.
But this is beside the point completely. Indeed, I resent the implicit suggestions that any French Canadian who cannot speak French has forsaken his cultural heritage or is some kind of traitor. I resent the suggestion that the well-being of French Canadians 20220-458
Canadian Flag
is totally tied up with the well-being of the province of Quebec.
I make these points, Mr. Speaker, because the myth is being circulated that all people of French descent support the expressions of view of a handful of extremists, some of whom are in this house. I have a right to speak for those French Canadians among us who do not live in Quebec, who do not speak French as their first language, who do not particularly feel that they have had an unfair deal, who do not resent the union jack or the red ensign, who do not consider the world wide use of English in commerce and international aviation as some sort of Anglo-Saxon plot against Quebec. Furthermore, I suggest that the widespread unease, anxiety and tension are being heightened by seemingly interminable demands on the part of some Quebec members, and more particularly by the startling inability of the government to manage the business of the house.
I urge the Prime Minister to use restraint in the course he has adopted, because the temper in the rest of Canada and indeed among many French Canadians in other parts of Canada is not good.
Who says so?

I say so. You listen, because I will have more to say. I urge the Prime Minister and the government to depart from the kind of tactic that we saw too often in the two previous election campaigns, the business of destroying something that is good before you can say you have anything else to offer. It was a matter of real concern to me to see the disrespect that became widespread with regard to the red ensign and the efforts, which I have to believe were conscious and deliberate, to discredit the red ensign among the young people of the country and in certain parts of the country as a preliminary step to introducing the three maple leaves pattern. I say get rid of this kind of tactic, because you will never achieve unity that way and you will only leave many of us in Canada with a bitter taste in our mouths.
The amendment and subamendment set out the terms of a plebiscite. Some speakers have suggested that a plebiscite would divide the country as it has never been divided before, but oddly enough these same speakers feel that a vote in the House of Commons would not divide. I ask this question. Why in the world would anyone believe that feelings and emotions in the House of Commons would be less deep or less painful than in the country at large? Who is afraid to allow the

Canadian Flag
Canadian people the opportunity to say what they want in terms of a majority vote in a plebiscite?
I ask this question today particularly after the sham and the subterfuge has been stripped away from the public position of the Prime Minister on this whole question of the flag. I have wondered for weeks how there could be complete unanimity in the Liberal caucus over the flag issue. It was not until the confession of the hon. member for York-Humber yesterday that I realized why there was no disagreement. The matter had never been discussed with the membership of the caucus.
I urge the Prime Minister to reconsider this whole question, its timing and its dangers. There is after all, Mr. Speaker, a difference between courage and foolhardiness. I suggest that the course he is now following can only lead to a confrontation of all strong people, can only divide and deepen mistrust. If he does not do this, if he insists as he did earlier today that he shall have his way, then I predict that he will be remembered in history not as a man of many distinguished accomplishments and contributions to Canada, but rather as the great token prime minister who helped the country into bitterness that will he a lasting black mark on his name, on our House of Commons and on our time.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
I hesitated to rise, Mr. Speaker, because I did not want to prevent some member of the Liberal party from participating in the debate. I continue to wonder why no member of the cabinet has come to the defence of the Prime Minister. The Minister of Trade and Commerce was not doing that the other day. What has happened to the former great Liberal party?
However, as no one did rise, I take this opportunity to participate in what has become a great, historic debate of national importance. There is no question now, since ample evidence has been produced in the course of this debate, that there is a very strong feeling across this country against the action of the present government, and particularly the action of the Prime Minister. There has been ample evidence of the strength of feeling in members who have spoken so far in the course of this debate, and they have indicated that they are expressing the feelings of their constituents.
The miscalculation of the Prime Minister and his advisers has been shown to be very great. There was miscalculation with regard to the approach to a subject such as this
[Mr. Rhesume.)
which arouses the emotions, which affects our history and traditions; an amazing miscalculation with regard to the attitude that would be taken by the members of races other than the founding races of this country; a miscalculation with regard to the method by which an innovation like this should be brought forward.
This is a catalogue of errors. The result so far has been not to create the unity which the Prime Minister emphasized so much in his opening speech on this subject, but to create great disunity. The Prime Minister will go down in history as the man who, of his own accord, by his own faulty judgment, created greater disunity in this country than at any time in our history. This is a lamentable development indeed. I hope it is not too late for the Prime Minister to retrace his steps and restore to Canada better feeling with regard to the matters that should unite us rather than divide us.
In a matter such as this, as the hon. member for Brandon-Souris pointed out when he was speaking, evolution is the process, a slow and steady development if change is desired in something that touches so deeply at the roots of our country, and not the revolutionary tactics and arbitrary action of the government. This was the initial, vital mistake of the Prime Minister. His greatest error was made in his approach to the biennial conference of the Royal Canadian Legion in May of this year in the city of Winnipeg. Members of the Royal Canadian Legion will take second place to no citizens of this country in their devotion to duty and their love of their country. They have demonstrated this ever since the organization of that great body. Their efforts are primarily concentrated, after they have dealt with the problems of their disabled comrades, on improving the life of communities right across Canada and making stronger our national spirit.
However, it was to this body that the Prime Minister, without prior notice, without advising the officers of that organization that he was going to introduce a political note, brought forward his proposal for a new flag. As a member of the Legion since 1927 I register, as my comrades on this side of the house have, my protest against that action. When I heard that the Prime Minister was going out to Winnipeg to do this-and in this rumour-infested town you hear about these things in advance-I said it would not happen for three reasons. First, the Prime Minister is himself a veteran of the first

world war. He will respect the stand of the veterans on the question of the flag. He knows they have been endeavouring to conduct a campaign to retain the Canadian red ensign. In the second place, he will not do it because, as a veteran, he knows that their opening ceremony held on Sunday is a memorial service, a deeply impressive memorial service, for the hundred thousand comrades who were left overseas around the world. I said that he would know every man and woman in that audience on that occasion would be thinking of friends who had been lost in battle. I said the third reason he would not do it would be that, after years of experience in the field of diplomacy and in political life, he would judge it to be unwise to introduce a political question under such circumstances.
Unfortunately the Prime Minister, either wrongly advised or failing to exercise good judgment, intruded himself upon that memorial service of the Canadian Legion and introduced a political tone that aroused controversy which will not be forgotten. Unfortunately the Prime Minister-and this is really unfortunate because veterans tend to respect veterans-lost the respect of thousands of members of the Canadian Legion. To show how much effect his announcement had on this gathering, in subsequent days when they were still assembled in their business sessions, a petition addressed to the Secretary of State was signed with 1,100 names, indicating the veterans were unimpressed with the Prime Minister's point of view and registering their opinion and belief that the Canadian red ensign should be maintained as Canada's flag. I shall transmit that petition to the Secretary of State as a permanent record of the feelings of the members of the Canadian Legion who were present at that meeting.
I intend to deal with certain inaccuracies which have crept into this debate, concerning the maple leaf emblem and the Canadian red ensign, and then I propose to indicate why in the suggested plebiscite, if and when it is held, people should give their support to the flag we now have rather than to the personal choice of the Prime Minister or to the personal choice of a fragment of the New Democratic party, because you have in those two suggestions political flags, flags sponsored by political parties. With regard to the inaccuracies that have crept into the debate so far, much has been made of the fact that the maple leaf has a long history in our country, and with that I do not disagree. The hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson), who patiently made quite a study of this matter, 20220-458J
Canadian Flag
pointed that out when he was talking. It has been a recognized symbol and, as I said during the course of his speech, we admire it as a symbol but not as a flag.
I do not quarrel with any of the arguments made about the antiquity of the maple leaf as a Canadian symbol, but I do suggest that the references made by the hon. member for Leeds and the Prime Minister, with regard to its use by the Canadian army overseas and Canadian service people overseas in two world wars, are somewhat inaccurate.
Quite a bit was made of the fact that most of the battalions that served overseas in the first world war wore the maple leaf as a cap badge or shoulder badge. That is true because about 90 per cent of them did; but I happen to be one, like the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Fane), who served in that world war and never wore a maple leaf badge. There were thousands of others also in a similar position. However most of the battalions did have a maple leaf badge, and it arose this way.
When mobilization was called in 1914 General Sir Sam Hughes, minister of national defence, decided he would not use the names of the militia regiments and favoured instead, and so ordered, that regiments would be numbered. So the battalions that were raised were numbered from one up to several hundred. Then, when the battalions were being organized the commanding officers were faced with a considerable problem, one which I have gone through twice in my experience in the army, namely what to do for a cap badge, what should be the design, and what to do with a number, like 7, 44 or 115, pinned to the cap. The obvious solution was to put a backing on the cap badge, and the easiest thing to deal with was a maple leaf. And so the maple leaf was used as a base and the numbers were superimposed on it.
There were a few exceptions. The Little Black Devils of Winnipeg did not put the maple leaf behind their historic figure. The 22nd regiment superimposed their number on the beaver, and the Black Watch maintained their original insignia. The Fort Garry Horse of Winnipeg had the Fort Garry gate, and they put the maple leaf behind that; but they should now remove it because the Fort Garry gate alone is sufficient recognition of that regiment. Neither did the Royal Canadian Dragoons make use of the maple leaf. And so it was by accident, not by design, that the maple leaf was so outstanding and so extensively used in the first world war.
In the second world war about 60 per cent of the battalions in the army used the maple

Canadian Flag
leaf in connection with their badges, and 40 per cent did not. Once again in my experience in the second world war I served in northwest Europe without wearing anything resembling a maple leaf, and so did thousands of other members of the Canadian army, the Royal Canadian Air Force and the navy. In the second world war the maple leaf was not the all-pervading symbol that it was in the first world war, and in the regular army of today only about 20 per cent of the battalions have a maple leaf incorporated in the design of their badges. Therefore the maple leaf has been going out of existence since the first world war, when it arose by accident, and you cannot make an argument on the basis of war experience that the maple leaf was preferred by Canadian servicemen.
To give the house an example of how misconceptions arise, in the fall of 1945 some parliamentarians visited northwest Europe. They motored up from the Normandy beaches into Holland, and by that time the army was forward in Holland and on the banks of the Meuse. These parliamentarians were impressed by what they saw en route and one of them made the following remarks a few years ago, after indicating where they had been. As a matter of fact they did not drive up from the Normandy beaches. They flew into Brussels, motored down the coastline and then up into Holland; but this is what he says about the Canadian troops:
As if they were anxious to show that they were Canadians they had painted maple leaves on pieces of cardboard, and nailed them to the telegraph poles and trees along the road. If up to that time I had not believed that Canada should have a distinctive flag, I would have believed it then. And ever since that time, whenever, I have had the opportunity I have told that story, because I think it meets some of the arguments of those who think that we should not consider having a purely distinctive national flag.
It is very easy for misconceptions to arise when you do not know the facts. The fighting troops of the Canadian army were much further forward than these visiting parliamentarians. The parliamentarians travelled along a route which was marked with maple leaf emblems from the Normandy beaches into Holland, and the purpose of those markings was simply to direct the lorry drivers on that long drive, travelling night and day, so that they would not have to stop to read maps. We called it "maple leaf up" and "maple leaf down". Those signs were just road signs set up by ingenious Canadians for that purpose, and they were of great help to a lorry driver I had in my regiment who

was unable to read or write, but who could follow the signs.
One of the visiting parliamentarians thought this was evidence of a national desire on the part of the Canadian troops to have the maple leaf as their symbol. But there was nothing to it at all. It was simply a route director and the Canadian soldiers paid no more attention to this than they did to a great many other things during their lives. As a matter of fact, in both world wars the distinguishing sign for Canadians was the word "Canada" on the shoulder, worn on the greatcoat or on the tunic. You don't peer at a man's cap badge to find out what country he comes from; you look at the flash on his shoulder. Every Canadian was proud to have the word "Canada" there, and that is how they were designated. In forward areas, where steel helmets were worn, there were no cap badges in evidence. It was the distinguishing regimental flash, the brigade and divisional insignia on the arm of the tunic, which indicated where a man belonged.
But every divisional badge contained a maple leaf.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
No. In the first world war there were 140 badges and these will be found in the official history of that war. They were of different colours, and there is not a maple leaf to be found among them.
Another inaccuracy which has crept into this debate is the statement of the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) as reported on page 4321 of Hansard:
The red ensign, though many of my correspondents do not seem to appreciate this, was not in use during world war one in any way, shape or form for the Canadian forces.
I do not know where the Prime Minister served during the first world war but I think it was not in Flanders. He must have been completely unaware of what was going on. Yesterday my hon. friend from Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan), imperturbable as he must have been as an artillery man in the first world war, showed equal impertur-bility here under a missile attack in the House of Commons and gave incontrovertible evidence that the Canadian red ensign was used among Canadian troops between 1914 and 1918, and backed his statements up with testimony from General McNaughton. I can corroborate this story, because I was present also, on July 1, Dominion day, at the corps sports event which everyone who was there

will remember all his life. On that occasion, Canadian red ensigns were flying freely at our assembly points.
Was the Canadian red ensign used elsewhere in the first world war? Of course. In 1918 a monument was unveiled to the artillerymen who lost their lives during the battle of Vimy ridge and the Canadian red ensign was flown at the unveiling; a picture of it may be found in some of the books in the library. The Prime Minister did not make the long march from Mons to Germany to join the army of occupation. But I did. When we crossed the Rhine bridges, the first division crossing at Cologne and the second division at Bonn, we passed reviewing stands and on those stands the Canadian red ensign was flying with the union jack. I remember it very well, and as far as the bridge at Bonn is concerned, a reproduction appears in the August 1 edition of the Globe magazine-the second Canadian division passing the reviewing stand where the Canadian red ensign was flying. We experienced the same thing when the first Canadian division crossed the bridge at Cologne.
Let me remind the house of another significant factor. Earlier than this, in 1915, in the month of April, the Canadian first division- I was not there at the time-was subjected to a poison gas attack and fought the battle of St. Julien which prevented the Germans breaking through to Ypres and the coast. The name of Canada was spread throughout the world as a result of that action. This was the first occasion in the history of the world upon which poison gas had been used, and our Canadian troops were among the first to be subjected to it. They were without any protection whatsoever-it was before gas masks had been invented. And they held the line, though the Canadian division suffered 6,000 casualties, killed and wounded. But, as I say, the name of Canada was flashed across the world and in the celebrated magazine Punch, an artist, sensing the significance of that occasion, drew a picture which has since been reproduced many times in this country -it should be hanging somewhere in the corridors of our parliament buildings. It was a picture of a Canadian soldier standing on a battlefield amid barbed wire and mud; near him is a piece of artillery and all around is a scene of desolation and destruction. The soldier standing there holds a rifle in one hand, and in the other, he grasps-what? A Canadian red ensign-the distinctive flag of Canada at that time.

Hear, hear.

I mention these things to correct some of the inaccuracies which have crept into this debate thus far.
Another inaccuracy which is even more alarming is an inaccuracy with regard to Canada's coat of arms. The Prime Minister and the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Mathe-son) have based their case on the emblem of the three maple leaves which appears in the coat of arms, and they have drawn our attention to the proclamation of 1921. It is an incidental footnote to history that when this declaration was signed by King George in 1921 it was transmitted to Canada, to the governor general here, by none other than one who was a member of the government at that time, the most famous man of this century, Winston Churchill. His letter will be found in the appropriate books.
Hon. members opposite have spoken about that proclamation and they have based their case upon it. But they have been misled into inaccuracies. I do not think they realize the extent of those inaccuracies. On June 15, the Prime Minister, as recorded on page 4322 of Hansard, spoke on the subject of the proclamation and the order in council, and then he used these words:
If I may paraphrase this royal proclamation of 1921 establishing the arms of Canada, by simplifying the heraldic language, what it said in essence was this: The King, at the request of Canada, assigns to Canada the national colours white and red, and declares that the national emblem of Canada shall be three red maple leaves on one stem, on a white field. These shall be used to represent Canada on all appropriate occasions. Surely Mr. Speaker, that answers the two questions "What are our national colours"? "What is our national emblem"?
I suggest, first, that those words were not the original words of the Prime Minister; they are the words of Colonel Duguid, who delivered exactly that interpretation of the proclamation to the committee which was meeting in 1945 to discuss the Canadian flag. Those words, which I shall soon show to be inaccurate, have continued down for almost 20 years now, have received the blessing of the Prime Minister and are already being quoted as authentic by people who are writing letters to newspapers.

Mr. Speaker, I will but interrupt my hon. friend for a moment, but I wonder whether at this point he would be good enough to explain the answer given by his government on February 5, 1963, to question No. 1,449. This question was:
Does Canada have a national emblem; and If so, what is the emblem?

The answer was:
Yes. Three maple leaves conjoined on one stem.
The other question was:
Does Canada have national colours; and if so, what are these colours?
Yes. White and red.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
I am very glad the hon. member mentioned that, Mr. Speaker, because he has been studying this problem and his speech in June encouraged me to study it. I would say now that the government of our day was misled, in exactly the same way as was the government of Mr. Mackenzie King, the government of Mr. St. Laurent, and the present government. I shall give the house the evidence to show this is the case. I will put forward two pieces of evidence. One is contained in the committee report of 1945 and is to be found on page 59. Mr. Savage, who is not without distinction in the art of heraldry, made these statements. He said that Colonel Duguid's statement abounds in false premises and inaccuracies; that Colonel Duguid has confounded the colours of mantling and crest wreath with "national colours"; has taken the maple sprig, a small part of Canada's arms, and incorrectly stated that it is the "national emblem of Canada". Then Mr. Savage says in so doing Colonel Duguid has changed from green to red the accepted and heraldically proper colour of the maple leaves; has read into and deduced from the proclamation, and has presented as facts, conclusions and statements which definitely are not included in that document.
As further evidence let me draw to the attention of the house the explanatory notes that were produced by the committee of 1921. The committee, which the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson) has drawn to our attention, and has commended for its ability- with which I do not disagree at all, because very able men sat on that committee-made certain comments in their explanatory notes concerning the coat of arms. You have to refer to a bulletin of the dominion bureau of statistics in order to find what they had to say. I have been able to find only the second edition of a descriptive booklet published by the office of the secretary of state in 1923. There was obviously a first edition. There have been subsequent editions published, I think, in 1937 and 1947. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I had to go back to the d.b.s. annual report of 1921 to find out what they had decided was the meaning of that proclamation and the advice they had given to the government. This is

what you will find on page 17 of the Canada Year Book of 1921:
Three considerations were kept in view in determining the "achievement of arms", i.e., the combination of arms, crest, supporters and motto, which has now been authorized. These were: first, that Canadians stand to their King in as close a relation as do any of his subjects elsewhere: secondly, that Canada, an integral part of the British empire, has emerged from the war a member of the league of nations; and lastly, that Canada was founded by the men of four different races-French, English, Scottish and Irish-and that Canadians inherit the language, laws, literature and arms of all four mother countries.
The arms are those of England, Scotland, Ireland, and France, with a "difference" to mark them as Canadian, namely, on the lower third of the shield, a sprig of maple on a silver shield.
The crest is a lion holding in its paw a red maple leaf, a symbol of sacrifice.
The supporters are, with some slight distinctions, the lion and unicorn of the royal arms. The lion upholds the union jack, and the unicorn the ancient banner of France.
The motto is new-A mari usaue ad mare-"From Sea to Sea''...
There is not one word there with regard to national colours. Are we to believe that the committee which sat in 1921, and which subsequently drew up the representations for the coat of arms and had the coat of arms produced and submitted to the college of heralds in London, were dealing with national colours when they went through all that work? Why did they not make some mention of "national colours" in the course of their explanatory notes? Why is there no mention of this in the subsequent issues? In this issue there is not one word about "national colours". I ask the hon. member for Leeds, who has made a study of this problem, to indicate to me the authority by which he determined that the mantling on the coat of arms represents national colours. I have not been able to find any authority for that.
Mr. Speaker, if I may-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I do not mind these interruptions, Mr. Speaker, provided my time is not subsequently reduced, because it is a very interesting question. I think our government was misled, just as other governments were misled, by that original statement of Colonel Duguid's. Let me deal now with the three red maple leaves. I have read the description that on the coat of arms there is a lion standing on the crest, holding in an uplifted paw a red maple leaf. The explanation is, "The crest is a lion holding in its paw a red maple leaf, a symbol of sacrifice". That description or definition was repeated in the subsequent issues concerning the arms of Canada, published by the office of the Secretary of State, until you reach the issue of this year, 1964, when that descriptive sentence is left out.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Why was it left out? In the terminology of the coat of arms this red leaf is described as "gules", which means red. There were three other leaves in the coat of arms and the description, I think, can be given as "proper", or in the French version, "au naturel", which means in its natural state. The red maple leaf had been pre-empted for one specific purpose, to indicate the sacrifice of life in the first world war which contributed to the building of our nation.
We cannot have then, sir, one red maple leaf representing that sacrifice and then three more red maple leaves. That was never intended, because had the people who devised the coat of arms in 1921 intended that the three leaves at the bottom should be red they would have specifically stated that and used the word "gules". They did not use that word but instead "proper" or "au naturel". The maple leaf in its natural state is green. It is when the leaf is dying that it turns red.
Canadian Flag
Are we to take away from the coat of arms, as has been taken away in this descriptive booklet, that red maple leaf which represents a blood sacrifice in the first world war? I say that Colonel Duguid was wrong when he said that the three maple leaves at the lower part of the coat of arms should be red. He was obviously aiming at the achievement of something; a white background for a flag with red maple leaves.
We are now faced with this problem. What do we do with the coat of arms? If we are going to accept the idea of three red maple leaves on a white background in the coat of arms, what do we do with the red maple leaf in the right paw of the lion representing that sacrifice? You see, this is an impossible situation. I suggest this change was made for some deliberate purpose.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader

I am surprised that members opposite laugh. I think that red maple leaf representing the sacrifice made in the first world war is very proper and should be retained. I think, therefore, we should revert to the colour which was on the crest before, namely three green maple leaves.
Referring again to the original question asked by the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson), Mr. Speaker, I think that the secretary of state in 1957 was misled or not given complete information. As a matter of fact, I phoned her to find out what the situation was, but my only recollection of that episode is that we were told the coat of arms would be changed because Queen Elizabeth had selected a different crown; the St. Edward crown to replace the Tudor crown. The only alteration required in the coat of arms was a redrawing of the crown, and that was done.
That opened the way to what has been called a simplification of the coat of arms. I do not object to this and I think it has been done rather nicely. However, in the circular letter-there was no order in council- issued on September 23, 1957 and signed by the under secretary of state, there was nothing to indicate that there would be changes made in the coat of arms. There was reference to the fact that the change was being made because of the change of crown, and I think this is sensible. There was also reference to simplifying representations of the coat of arms but not one word in respect of changing the green maple leaves to red.
Mr. Speaker, when the enlarged coat of arms was hung up in the railway committee room several years ago I looked at it week

Mr. Michener, and asked whether steps could be taken to have that coat of arms coloured so we could see exactly what was on it. Had it been coloured I am sure I would have noticed the change from green to red.
Mr. Speaker, I suggest an error has been committed, and the reason I have dealt with this matter at length is that unless this error is corrected people outside this House of Commons, writing about our coat of arms and our so-called national colours, will follow this mistaken course. I feel this error should be corrected.
Mr. Speaker, I could produce more evidence from people skilled in heraldry to support my point of view. I think it would be a great advantage to a committee to consider this problem and to call for expert advice. We are amateurs in heraldry. I did not know much about it three months ago, although I know a lot more about it today. But we are only amateurs. Furthermore, the revised coat of arms issued in 1957 was not submitted to the college of heralds in London, and there is no college of heralds in Canada. It was not submitted for their advice, counsel and approval as to whether or not this design was accurate. I suggest we have fallen into an error. We are referring to Canada's colours being white and red. I say there is no authority for that suggestion. We are talking about Canada's national emblem being three red maple leaves on a silver-white background. I say there is no authority for that suggestion whatsoever, except that statement made by Colonel Duguid in 1945.

Mr. Speaker, I originally had no intention of entering this debate on the flag, but after so many opposition members stating that the backbenchers in the Liberal party should get up and state their opinions I concluded that I should do so, and give my reasons for the position I take. It is not against my conscience that I do so, Mr. Speaker.
First let me say I am a Canadian, a Legion member and a past president of my local Legion branch. I am a life member of the Legion and I served in the first great war under the union flag or, as it is called, the union jack. Sometimes I think I belong to the lost generation, the generation of the union jack. All these things I do not think should keep me from thinking and stating that Canada should have a distinctive flag.
As a Canadian, my ancestors have been here for upwards of 200 years. Before the first great war I was what you might call a Britisher-not an Englishman, Mr. Speaker,

but a Britisher. Canada was a part of the empire and I was a British subject. For me, when the empire was at war Canada was at war. At that time I was not alone in those thoughts. Sir Wilfrid Laurier was an ardent champion of the empire. In fact, in 1898 his postmaster general brought out a stamp and the stamp showed the British empire all in red and Canada in the centre. The words on the stamp were, "We hold a vaster empire than has been". Even the Transvaal and the Orange Free State of South Africa were incorporated in red, although I believe they were not annexed by Britain until two years later.
For many reasons the first great war changed the opinions and ideas of a great many people, and after the war for me Canada came first. On returning home I thought in the words of the poet:
Breathes there the man, with soul so dead,
Who never to himself hath said,
This is my own, my native land?
If I was not before, Mr. Speaker, I was a Canadian then; but the union jack was still my flag. It has been said by opposition members that the cross of St. George, the cross of St. Andrew and the cross of St. Patrick, together forming the union jack, have always stood for high ideals, justice and freedom and that in fact they represent our Christian faith. I would say that on balance in the past this was probably true. But what about a Scotsman whose forebears were forced out of Scotland under this same flag? Can he look back and, remembering the forced emigration from Scotland, the clansmen who were evicted from the highlands, the homes that were burned and the people who died on the emigration ships, think that that flag at that time represented high ideals, justice, freedom and the Christian faith for the highlanders? The hon. member for Pictou (Mr. MacEwan) can perhaps bear me out.
Reading John Prebble's "The Highland Clearances", one finds that in the summer of 1791 George Dunoon advertised the sailing of the Sarah and the Dove from Fort William in Scotland for Pictou, Nova Scotia. Had the laws then covering slave ships applied to these emigration vessels, they would not have been allowed to carry more than 489 passengers. Dunoon filled the tiny holds with 700 emigrants from Lord Reay's country and the clan lands of Seaforth, Fraser and Cameron. If they believed his promise that in Nova Scotia they would find a tree that supplied fuel, soap and sugar, they might have found the nightmare voyage endurable, but it is unlikely. Forty nine people died on the Sarah alone and the
Canadian Flag
suffering of all was so terrible that it was remembered in Nova Scotia for more than a century.
You might say, Mr. Speaker, why did they go? Well, the lairds or the chiefs of the clans owned the lands and they could not resist English money. The Scottish highlands were rented or bought up for sheep ranches. The people were evicted from their homes and if they did not move their homes were burned. They had to emigrate. It is surprising to me, Mr. Speaker, that so many of these people, including myself, still have a great love for their native land, Scotland, and for the flag which looked down on these terrible scenes. Perhaps it is because we can forget the past.
I heard a member of the opposition say that a country that forgets its past has no future, or words to that effect. However, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that most of the trouble in the world is because we cannot forget the past or do not wish to forget the past.
Look at the trouble on Cyprus, Mr. Speaker, the trouble on the Israeli border, the trouble in Kenya. In fact, it seems to me that the trouble all over the world is caused by people who cannot forget the past. My great-greatgrandfather was scalped by the French and Indians on a raid down the Saint John river, but I do not see that this is any reason for me to keep on remembering it so that I should hate all Frenchmen and all Indians. Apparently we were a bicultural people at that time.

Again, I heard an opposition member say that his father came to this country and found freedom. A great many people have come to this country and found freedom, but it was not always thus. We did not always have responsible government in Canada.
We do not have it now.

Louis Joseph Pa-pineau and William Mackenzie had to go to the United States. We had a rebellion in 1837. We did not always have responsible government in this Canada of ours. It was my great-grandfather and great-great-grandfather and many of the great-grandfathers of the members present who made this country and laid the foundations of freedom for those who came after to enjoy and for the present generation to enjoy.
It has been said by an opposition member that the Canadian red ensign is known all over the world as representing Canada, and is the only red ensign. I would point out that in 1939 there were six red ensigns. The British mercantile marine had one, Canada had one, Jamaica had one, British Guiana had one, Tasmania had one and Newfoundland had one. I have known the union jack and the red ensign for over 70 years and to my mind the red ensign has always been a secondary flag.
As of 1939, Pear's Encyclopedia states that the flag flown over Canadian government buildings outside Canada is the red ensign, but that inside Canada the union jack is used. Before the first great war we had no embassies abroad but after the war in the early thirties, I believe, embassies were established and there was no way to distinguish a Canadian embassy from a British embassy if they both flew the union jack, which was the flag of Canada. So apparently the secondary flag, the red ensign, was flown over these buildings. Hence Pear's Encyclopedia states that in 1939 the red ensign was flown over Canadian government buildings outside Canada and by the Canadian mercantile marine, but inside Canada the union jack was used.
The union flag was introduced in 1606 after the union of England and Scotland and first bore the crosses of St. George and St. Andrew. It was ordered by James I to be borne on the maintop of all British ships except ships of war. On ships of war the union flag was borne upon their jackstaffs.
I believe this is the reason why it is called 

the union jack. The cross of St. Patrick was added in 1801 on the union with Ireland.
Now, Mr. Speaker, there are three ensigns and the ensign is flown upon the ensign staff of the vessel indicating its nationality. The red, white and blue ensigns represented the divisions of the British fleet but in 1864 the divisions were done away with and new uses were allocated to the three ensigns. The white ensign is the exclusive flag of the Royal Navy and the Royal Yacht Squadron. The red ensign is flown by British merchant ships and ships not belonging to the Royal Navy. The blue ensign is flown by the Royal Naval Reserve and by certain yacht clubs.
The Cambridge Encyclopedia states that colonial war vessels flew the blue ensign with the colony's badge in the fly. Recently I made a voyage on a Canadian government fishery vessel to Campobello and I noticed that the vessel flew the blue ensign and it had a badge in the fly, I presume denoting the colony. I would also point out that in Jamaica the flag with the crosses flew for nearly 300 years, 100 years longer than in Canada. When Jamaica became independent this flag, which had represented the power and prestige of the British for 300 years, was pulled down or lowered not by a citizen of Jamaica but by a member of the royal family, Princess Margaret. I would point out also, Mr. Speaker, that the blue ensign, the flag of Kenya, was pulled down or lowered not by a citizen of Kenya but by a member of the royal family, Prince Philip. Can the opposition be more loyal to the crown than the royal family itself?
It has been said by members of the opposition that the crosses on our flag represent the Christian faith and the government is engaged in pulling down the Chistian faith; that they are apparently about to raise a non-Christian flag. Some rather vicious propaganda has come across my desk in this regard. In one propaganda sheet headed, "The Sign of the Times", it states:
Christian haters have taken the cross off the soldiers' graves, so take the cross off the flag- the next will be the cross out of the churches.
I do not believe that any member in this house would agree that this is true. I would point to the Irish republic, a Christian state from early days and the emerald isle of St. Patrick. I suppose the Irishmen in the Irish republic are more Roman Catholic than the Roman Catholics themselves. Yet when they got a new flag, Mr. Speaker, did they put on it the cross of St. Patrick? No, they did not.

The Irish republic has a flag consisting of three stripes, green, white and orange. I can imagine that the green is for the emerald isle and the white is probably for honour or the Christian state. However the orange, that colour stumped me, unless it was put on for the orangemen of the six counties of northern Ireland with whom they wish to unite some time. The stripes are all of equal width, the green being nearest the pole. This argument, therefore, about Christianity and the flag seems to me to fall flat when we consider the flag of the Irish republic. In fact, many Christian countries have crosses on their flags and many Christian countries have not. Are we to say that the great republic to the south of us is not a Christian country because a cross does not appear on its flag?
I want a distinctive Canadian flag, Mr. Speaker. I have 12 grandchildren and I do not want them living in the past. I want them to live for the future. I want a distinctive Canadian flag for that future for them. Then, they and all other grandchildren in Canada can say, "This is my flag; this is the Canadian flag which represents the Canada of the future". Canada is a great country, Mr. Speaker. It is going to be still greater in thought, in word and in deed. I see the future of Canada in the bright, young and intelligent faces I look upon as I travel across our wonderful land.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. H. A. Thomas (Middlesex West):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since the day the session began this house has probably not faced a more important or a more serious decision than that concerning the new flag of this country. The flag, in itself, may not be important but that for which it stands is most important. Someone has said it represents the soul of the people, and I believe that. I believe that no amount of effort, no expense and no amount of time should stand in the way of this house choosing and offering the Canadian people a flag which will attain the unity of the people. Unity is needed in this country as much as anything else is needed. We have two great races that are undertaking to create, on the northern half of this continent, a great nation. Its future is almost unlimited. We have made a great start.
