There have been murmurings recently of discontent, a certain amount of bickering and quarrelling between the founding races of this country. I do not believe that this is serious, and after listening to the speeches in this debate I think that this house and the people of the country can take great hope
Canadian Flag
from what has transpired so far. The government, I honestly believe, has tried to add to the unity of Canada by presenting to the people a new Canadian flag, a distinctive flag, a flag which the people of Canada will be willing to accept as their own. I would commend the government for this, even although I think their approach to this problem is very wrong.
During one of the discussions of a recent budget the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) urged this house to give consideration to the objectives of the government, to take cognizance of what the government was trying to do, to give them credit for trying to improve the economy of this country. Well, I am willing to give the government credit for trying to create a greater measure of satisfaction in this country through the introduction of a flag.
Now we have before us a resolution, an amendment and a subamendment. The principle involved in the resolution is the establishment of a distinctive Canadian flag for Canada. I can agree with that. I can agree with most of the first sentence in the resolution which is to the effect that the government be authorized to take such steps as may be necessary to establish an official flag. I cannot agree with the remainder of it. The right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) has moved that all the words after "that" be deleted and the following substituted:
As the proposal to change Canada's national flag will affect the unity and destiny of Canada now and for years to come, the government be authorized to take such steps as may be necessary to conduct a plebiscite prior to any further action being taken by the House of Commons, in order that all Canadians may be given their rightful opportunity to declare their choice concerning a national flag.
Again, so far as the idea of a plebiscite is concerned, I am in wholehearted accord with it. I am speaking for myself when I say I question the words after the word "plebiscite" which are, "prior to any further action being taken by the House of Commons," and my reason for questioning that particular part of the amendment will be made clear as I go along.
The subamendment moved by the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. More) would seek to insert four questions in a plebiscite:
1.	Are you In favour of the Canadian red ensign?
2.	Are you in favour of the Canadian red ensign with changes made thereon to show the main heritages of both founding races?
3.	Are you in favour of the three maple leaves design?
4.	Are you in favour of a one maple leaf design?

Canadian Flag
I would like to see the people of Canada offered their choice in this regard, but I would not put these questions in words, I would put them in flag designs. The ballot would contain four, five or six of the most popular designs that can be arrived at through an all party committee or through a commission, and the people would be allowed to mark their "X" opposite the particular design of their choice. If that method were followed I see no reason why a flag design could not be arrived at and accepted which could be a unifying influence in this country.
Some people favour the red ensign; some favour three maple leaves, some favour one maple leaf. But there are other people who do not favour any of these and who are looking for something in the nature of a compromise, and that is the group which has my sympathy. If there is insistence on the unmodified red ensign there will be a large element dissatisfied. If the three maple leaf design is imposed by this house there will also be a great many people dissatisfied. It may be contended that you can never arrive at a design which will satisfy everybody, and I agree with that contention.
However I feel that the greatest amount of satisfaction and the greatest amount of unanimity can be reached through the acceptance of a flag which is acceptable to the majority of the people in this country. I have in my hand, and I suppose most members of the house have received this little flag, a design which may be folded, composed of a red cross and a blue cross arranged on a white background, with a maple leaf superimposed over the centre. This has been suggested by one of our colleagues from the province of Quebec. Another suggestion by one of our colleagues from Quebec is a flag divided diagonally from the upper outside comer to the lower inside corner, the upper inside triangle being red and containing a small union jack-quite small, not a quarter of the flag as it is in the red ensign-and the outside triangle, being white and containing a fleur-de-lis. I am only suggesting these as possible compromise flags which would tend to satisfy everyone and which would tend to unity rather than division.
The opposition has a job to do. Under the rules and traditions of parliament it is the duty and right of the opposition to prevent the government from taking action which might not be in the best interests of the country as a whole. The official opposition believes that the procedure-and I repeat the

word procedure-being used by the government in seeking to establish a new national flag is harmful to national unity and should be abandoned in favour of a different approach. The procedure being followed amounts to an autocratic imposition on the majority of Canadians against their will, and despite their protests, of a political, unilaterally chosen, unsatisfactory, party labelled flag.
A summer recess has been offered parliament as an incentive for acceptance, and a general election has been threatened for refusal. The stubborn persistence of the government in forcing this flag issue, in the way it is forcing it, has disrupted the orderly processes of parliament, has delayed the sessional program of legislation and is degrading the image of this institution. The government's methods have failed to promote unity and have failed to bring to the people of Canada the satisfaction that can rightfully be expected through the establishment of a distinctive, acceptable national flag.
The government's methods of approach have proved a failure. Widespread dissatisfaction and disunity have been the result. The time has come to adopt a new approach to this flag problem. The new approach suggested is the abandonment of the government's nation-wrecking, unity-destroying flag resolution in its present form, in favour of a continued search for other more satisfactory flag designs, through the medium of an all party committee, with the final choice to be made through a national plebiscite or referendum.
This is not a sudden unconsidered idea on my part. On February 24 I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) the following question on the orders of the day as shown on page 136 of Hansard:
In view of the government's undertaking to provide the people of Canada with a distinctive national flag, has consideration been given or will consideration he given to allowing the people to make their own choice through a plebiscite or referendum from among several of the most popular designs, including the red ensign?
To which the Prime Minister replied:
All I can say at the moment, Mr. Speaker, in regard to the procedure which should be followed in this matter is that parliament certainly should be put in a position to decide for or against a particular flag. As to whether it would be desirable to have a popular referendum on this matter so that the people could choose from among a number of designs, I would like to give that matter very careful consideration before agreeing to it.
I hope that as a result of this debate the Prime Minister can see his way clear to adopting such a course.

I have searched for the judgment of others to support my contention that the government is on the wrong track and in this regard I would refer the house to an editorial, already mentioned on several occasions during this debate, which appeared in the Globe and Mail some three months ago under the heading "Collision Course". It appeared in the issue of June 2, 1964. Even three months ago the editor who wrote this article could see where the situation was leading. The first paragraph reads as follows:
In his haste to give Canada a distinctive national flag, Prime Minister Lester Pearson has set his government and the nation itself on a collision course. There is still time for him to alter it. But there is not much time.
It seemed for a while during recent weeks as though an irresistible force had met an immoveable object. Something had to give. I am relieved, as I am sure all members of this house are relieved, that the government has seen the light to the extent that the threat of an election as a result of an adverse vote in the house has been rescinded. I believe the government has greatly increased its popularity by so doing. If they are willing to go the rest of the way and adopt an allparty approach to this flag issue, I am sure their stock will rise even higher. I am asking for a new approach through an all-party committee, the final selection from among several popular designs to be reached through a plebiscite or referendum.
The editorial article to which I have referred goes on to mention four errors the Prime Minister made in the method he used to provide Canada with a distinctive national flag. The first, the article says, was in setting a time limit of two years within which the new flag was to be produced. The second was to make the flag issue a question of confidence in the government, with a threat to dissolve parliament if the proposed new flag did not gain acceptance. Hon. members will recall that the Prime Minister started out with the idea of a free vote. He later changed his mind and made the issue a question of confidence. Now he is back to a free vote. We want him to change his mind further and make a new start altogether. By doing so he would make himself, his party, and the country generally, a lot happier.
The Prime Minister's third error, in the opinion of this editorial writer, was in giving the flag issue precedence over other pressing business in this house. On June 3, the day following the appearance of this article, the right hon. gentleman outlined 38 items of
Canadian Flag
business, passage of which was required before a summer recess. The flag resolution was not even mentioned. Yet 27 days later, by June 30, when the Prime Minister announced the final five or six items of legislation that he wished completed before a summer recess could be declared, this flag resolution had assumed such importance that it dominated the whole legislative program. The question is: What happened during the month of June to give the flag resolution such importance?
There have been some interesting speculations arising out of this question. One of them is that the flag issue was deliberately injected into the program in order to create a deadlock and provide an excuse for an election. If this was so, the bluff was called by the opposition. If the government wanted an election they were offered an opportunity to have one. Responsible members of this house will not be bought off or bluffed out of doing their job according to the dictates of their consciences.
The editorial writer in the Globe and Mail listed a fourth error. He said this was the bringing in of a doublebarrelled flag resolution covering both the government's design of three maple leaves and the union jack. By skilful use of the rule book the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) got the government out of that political sand-trap. The doublebarrelled resolution would have meant defeat in the house; government supporters would not have been willing to take the chance. This so-called fourth error lends further credence to the proposition that the government, for a time at least, was inviting defeat in order to justify an election.
However that may be, the situation was all changed as of Friday last when the Prime Minister lifted the election threat from the house and declared that any vote on the flag resolution or on the amendments thereto would be entirely free.
The Globe and Mail editorial writer ends with the following conclusion:
So we could have an election on, of all issues, a national flag. In such an election, we would be saying that the party with the most popular flag was the one best fitted to run the country. Canada should not-must not-get itself into this ludicrous and dangerous situation.
This is a time for statesmanship. Mr. Pearson should call in the leaders of the four opposition parties and thresh out the whole matter with them.
I am glad to say he has done that. The article goes on:
He should attempt to find agreement to a method of proceeding with the flag resolution that, by keeping the debate within bounds, would spare

Canadian Flag
the nation from being pitchforked into an election it does not want, on an issue that would threaten national unity.
I submit that editorial articles in the newspaper having the status of the Globe and Mail are worthy of consideration and it is my view that the contents of this article make good backing for the contention that the government is on the wrong track in its search for a national flag, and that the sooner it changes its approach the better it will be for all concerned. This editorial also supports strongly the proposition that the flag should not be a unilateral party choice but should be made an all-party project. We in this party are not asking that the government abandon their search for a satisfactory flag design. We are in favour of a distinctive national flag for Canada; a statement to that effect is in our party manifesto. What we are asking for and begging for, imploring, demanding and insisting upon, Mr. Speaker, is that the government cease its unilateral party policy and adopt an all-party approach.
I submit that the government is fully aware that they are being somewhat stubborn in this matter. As proof of their stubborn attitude, consider one paragraph of the Prime Minister's speech of June 30, as reported at page 4906 of Hansard. He said:
The government has been urged to postpone the flag resolution-
I may say, Mr. Speaker, that the Prime Minister was discussing the legislation which should be completed before a possible summer recess. This was at the time when he was suggesting there were 38 or 40 different pieces of legislation to be dealt with. He said:
The government has been urged to postpone the flag resolution, as it is obstructing other legislation and as it is, as we all admit, a measure which is controversial and arouses deep and genuine emotions. So far as obstructing other legislation is concerned, I think it is quite clear that there never will be a time when this flag issue, which is an issue of vital national importance, will not be controversial and will not interfere with other legislative proposals to which some hon. members would, for various reasons, wish to give priority over it. So, whenever this resolution would be introduced in the house there would be that difficulty.
I would say, Mr. Speaker, that if the government would stop being stubborn over having their own way in this matter, and would adopt an all-party approach and give up their high pressure rush, their troubles with regard to a flag would disappear and a greater measure of unity could be achieved. In spite of warnings and protests in parliament and from outside, the Prime Minister has consistently refused to alter his approach

to the flag issue. He has stated time and again in the house that the flag resolution must be carried through to a decision before a summer recess can be allowed. Well, the time is getting rather late for a summer recess; I am afraid it will have to be a Christmas recess. In his June 30 speech the Prime Minister made another statement, as is reported at page 4907 of Hansard. He was still speaking of the items of legislation which he said should be completed before a summer recess could be declared:
In any event, when the matters I have mentioned are dealt with, we shall return to the flag resolutions and the debate on those resolutions would be continued until a decision is reached on them.
He went on further to say:
The target date I should like to submit is the end of July. If we meet that target date it would be our desire and, I think, the desire of all members of the house, for parliament to recess until the middle of September.
It is rather sad to consider those words in retrospect, Mr. Speaker. Here we have the bribe and the threat; the bribe of a recess if the resolution is accepted; the threat that there would be no end to this session short of dissolution, because the Prime Minister must know full well that there are many members in this house who are not prepared to accept the proposition that a unilaterally chosen, party labelled flag shall be imposed as a national symbol on the people of Canada, against the will of a majority and despite their protests.
As further support for the suggested remedy that we are seeking in this matter, I submit the contents of a letter from 12 responsible citizens who have attained a status in their various fields of work which entitles their collective opinion to the fullest consideration. This letter is addressed to the Prime Minister under date of May 27, 1964. I believe copies of this letter were forwarded to every member of this house; at least, I received a copy. Its contents are endorsed by Dr. D. G. Creighton, professor of history at the University of Toronto; Dr. Eugene Forsey, director of research of the Canadian Labour Congress; Mrs. H. A. Dyde, of Edmonton; Dr. W. L. Morton, professor of history, University of Manitoba; Mr. T. H. B. Symons, president and vice-chancellor, Trent university; Mr. Jean Palardy, author, Montreal; Dr. Denis Smith, assistant professor of politics, Trent University; David M. Harley, barrister and solicitor, Toronto; Eric McLean, music critic, Montreal; Mr. Walter Pitman, a respected exmember of this house-
Hear, hear.

I am glad to see that some of his colleagues remember him. He is head of the history department of Kenner collegiate, Peterborough; Dr. Macgregor Parsons, Red Deer, Alberta; Mr. Scott Symons, assistant curator in charge of Canadiana Collections, Royal Ontario Museum. The letter is not long, but I fear I shall not have time to read it. I will leave it till later, Mr. Speaker, and read it if I do have time. However, I should like to put the last paragraph on the record at this time:
We respectfully suggest that you withdraw the maple leaf design for the time being, and that you convoke at once a private meeting of the parliamentary leaders of all parties to agree upon a new design which asserts our history. We profoundly believe that the present proposal will only deepen the spiritual malaise of Canada.
I consider this to be one of the finest analyses I have seen regarding the Canadian flag. I will read the rest of that letter, if there is time, before I finish. I wish to submit, as further evidence of dissatisfaction with the government's course of action, an editorial in the July 24 issue of the Montreal Gazette, which reads as follows:
Though a new Canadian flag is far from having been officially adopted, it has been flown a good deal across Canada in an unofficial way. Canadians have had the opportunity to see it as a flag, not merely as a design. And it must be said that it is a poor looking flag. Whatever may be said about the flag issue in general, this particular flag lacks life and colour; it is a drab thing, scrawny and weak.
It is not altogether surprising that the product is poor. For though Canada has had years to contemplate designs for flags, the particular design selected by the government in the end was drawn in a curious crash program.
The designers did their work in nine hectic days. The flag that won the cabinet's approval (with slight later changes) was that of a retired commander of the Royal Canadian Navy, who regards himself as an enthusiastic amateur in the field of heraldry. He worked, as he says, "with one eye closed from 10.30 at night until shortly after 1.30 in the morning."
The design shows rather sadly the one-eyed rush and fatigue with which it was conceived. Not even those most enthusiastic for a new flag have been able to show an equal enthusiasm about the design proposed. These three scratchy maple leaves, dying on a severed stem, have been flown enough already, in an unofficial way, to make clear that they can respond to even a bracing breeze with nothing but a dismal flap.
Mr. Speaker, that is a further indication in a responsible newspaper editorial, as evidenced by the policy of that newspaper, that the present proposed flag does not command the unanimity and the sympathy of the people of this country.
Canadian Flag
I have received hundreds of letters on this flag issue, as I expect have all members of this house. Hundreds of these letters from Legion groups, the daughters of the empire, Canadian corps associations, women's institutes and others are in favour of the red ensign. Hundreds of other letters are in favour of the government's flag and other designs.
I am opposed to allowing the government to continue on a course of action which will tend to divide the people of Canada into two groups, and then to chose between them in such a way that for generations to come one half of the people of Canada will have bitter feelings towards the other half.
The government's proposal will not bring unity, but discord, and there is no sound reason why they should continue to follow such a policy in such a rush. I believe that a flag design can be chosen through the employment of the proposed methods, which will be more acceptable to all, and in the choice of which there will be no winners and no losers, and from which will result national unity rather than division.
In dealing with the flag issue this house is playing for keeps. I should like to stress that fact, Mr. Speaker. If we discard the red ensign and what might be a compromise flag, and the present resolution succeeds in passing this house, as it appears it will at this stage if there is a vote, we will not be able to undo what we will have done. If we take a sensible attitude we will not be able to undo our actions because we cannot have a new flag every time the government changes. I repeat, no amount of effort, expense, trouble or time should be allowed to stand in the way of the choice of a flag which will be acceptable and tend to unify this country. I think it is possible to find such a design if we adopt an all party approach and let the people make their own choice. For that reason I am in support of the principle of the subamendment as well as, I may say, part of the amendment and part of the resolution.
Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to comment on some of the remarks made by several hon. members who have preceded me in this debate. I was particularly interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill), who dealt with the history of the maple leaf both in France and during the last war.
I remember being ordered toward the end of the last war to wear the maple leaf insignia on my tunic. If my memory serves me

Canadian Flag
correctly only certain troops were instructed to wear that insignia, and those were army troops such as ordnance and supply. I do not believe that the members of regiments who formed the fighting force were ordered to wear the maple leaf patch. When the troops who were ordered to wear this patch saw the design there was an expression of disgust, distaste and annoyance. The patches consisted of a golden maple leaf within a dark circle, to be worn on the shoulder. They were considered to be very ugly in design, and I remember that we could not understand why we should be forced to wear them. I am sure they were worn only because of a threat of military punishment. There was such resentment that quite a long time after the order was issued, at a party in the officers' mess at headquarters, a senior officer pointed out to a brigadier that practically none of his officers were wearing this insignia on their uniforms as required. I assure you there was a good deal of trouble about this situation, and one result was a parade at eight o'clock the following morning of the entire officer group of that unit. I presume this parade was held in an attempt to make sure that the maple leaf patch was worn on the tunics of those officers. I might add, that unit was the largest in the Canadian army.
Mr. Speaker, I point out these facts to give some indication of the reaction to the order requiring these particular army troops to wear that maple leaf insignia. I remembered this situation again only when the hon. member for "Winnipeg South Centre referred to the maple leaf insignia being used for various purposes at various times.
It is perhaps because I grew up in western Canada that I cannot understand why the maple leaf is supposed to be significant and emblematic of Canada. The use of the insignia to which I referred was introduced only late in the last war, and only to a limited degree. So far as the outfit, to which I was attached, is concerned, it met with nothing less than resentment.
It was a pleasure to hear the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre describe the use of the maple leaf to indicate wartime truck routes. I have never before heard anyone attempt to twist the meaning and acceptance of the use of the maple leaf insignia during the last war into a suggestion that there was a great demand for its use by Canadian troops. I have never heard the significance of the use of that insignia by Canadian troops referred to as a demand for the replacement

of our national flag by a flag including that particular design.
Mr. Speaker, in view of the great propaganda campaign, and the attempt to stir up the feelings of Canadian people by misrepresentation, as well as the attempt to minimize the agitation that has been created, I feel it is essential to bring these misrepresentations to light whenever an opportunity presents itself.
I was much intrigued by the remarks of the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. McLean), and I must say I have a good deal of respect for that hon. member. He certainly spoke with conviction. However, I think it is incredible that a man of his age will state, as did some other members in the far left corner of this chamber, that we should not consider the past at all but only look to the future. If any member asks, what is Canada today, I am sure the answer can only be found in our history, those things that Canada has done, the opportunities that have been given to people in this country, the actions that Canadians as individuals and as a nation have taken throughout the years. Canada is a land with a reputation for upholding its end in international obligations, but we have to look at history to see that we have taken our share in world conflicts and world conferences and have made our time, money and resources available to help others.
I certainly hope the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. McLean) is not suggesting that we should not look back and recall these things when somebody asks what Canada is today. I think it would be a betrayal of every soldier who ever fought with distinction in a Canadian uniform to say that we should not look back if the question is asked, what is Canada. If it is not the sacrifices of those men who fought in two world wars, the Korean war and the South African war, if our history of valour on the field of battle and in defence of democracy is not a part of present day Canada, then I do not know what is.
Certainly those who say we should only look to the future must have their tongues in their cheeks. Canada's future is bright and promising but it has been made so only because of the achievements of the past. I suggest that the hon. member for Charlotte and others who are taking a specious look at the question and saying we should forget the past and look only to the future have no idea how to look to the future. They have not, unless they take into consideration what our parliamentary institutions are based on, what our history of democracy and our system of justice mean. Unless they look to the past and understand

it they have no conception of the manner in which we should proceed in the future. _
In the thinking of some hon. members who say that a new flag is something of the future and that we should quit looking at the past,
I suggest we can put our finger on one of the misconceptions that may have caused this house and the whole country so much trouble in considering the question of whether we should now change our national flag completely. I should not have to remind members that there have been instances such as in Germany during the 1930's when there has been a failure to realize what the system of democracy is based on. Spurious claims and some flag waving were made use of to divert the attention of the people of that country from the lessons of the past, with the result that they lost their democracy. If those who resist most strongly a change in our national flag base their argument solely on the premise that the union jack and the red ensign stand for our history of democratic government, for the achievement of our nationhood and as a reminder of our parliamentary system and our system of justice, and take the stand that it is necessary to keep these reminders in front of us in order that people like the hon. member for Charlotte will not forget the importance of the past, then I think we have an almost undefeatable argument.
I must say that since the flag debate first began I have resented the efforts made in the house and throughout the country to say that we have no flag. Efforts have been made to say that the red ensign is not distinctive and that it has never really been Canada's flag. I thought the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Harkness) did the house and the country a real service when he pointed out in his speech that the red ensign has in fact been Canada's national flag for 100 years. For the life of me I cannot understand why some members keep saying in this debate that we must get a national flag. Certainly the question is whether we now want to change our national flag, and the more people say we must get one the more they are adding to that type of propaganda which has been foisted upon the people to mislead them into thinking that Canada does not now have a national flag.
I have just been home for a week end, for a change, and had a chance to speak to quite a group of people. It was one of the largest gatherings I have attended since I came here in January, and after such a long while I found it most refreshing to have a chance to hear people speak very bluntly and simply about what is going on in this chamber these
Canadian Flag
days, express their feelings about the flag debate and about whether they want a new flag, or the present flag changed. I am not going to pretend there is anything like unanimity on this matter. I believe that the strongest feeling throughout the country is: Why is parliament fooling around with the flag? Why does it not get on with the business? I think that is a fair summation of the majority feeling that I encountered at home.
There are quite a number who do not become vehement about the red ensign or the new flag and who in fact care very little about the matter, except to the extent that the present argument may disrupt the country. These people cannot understand why the subject has been brought up now. They cannot understand why it has taken so much time and why other business has not been proceeded with. I think there are some questions that the government owes it to the country to answer. I have talked to other members and I find that the situation in my constituency is not much different from that in other constituencies. Certainly the newspapers reflect the situation to quite an extent. I would say there is a general feeling across the country that the flag debate is interfering with more important business and there is an inability to understand why this is so.
I have asked the Prime Minister before, as have other hon. members, to explain why it is necessary that the flag debate should go through to a conclusion now. We have had the red ensign for 100 years. Certainly there is no doubt in the minds of most members of the house that, improperly handled, this subject can do more to destroy unity in this country than any other action of this or previous governments. Why then must it be rammed through with such haste? If those people who are so desirous of having a national flag and who put all the pressure they can on the government really want one that much, if it means that much to them, then it should be so important to them that they would not begrudge the time necessary to make sure that it is done properly and that the matter is handled in such a manner that it will bring credit, not only on any new national flag but on the people who support it and on the manner in which it was introduced.
Certainly, Mr. Speaker, I know if I were one of those who desired to get rid of the red ensign-and there is a certain group in this country who do not care what the new flag is as long as it is not the red ensign and has no union jack on it-I am sure I would say.

Canadian Flag
let us make sure we put this over in such a way that it will not be resented; it must stand for a feeling of unity in the country; it must be a unifying force. We do not want it taken as a symbol of our dissatisfaction or as evidence of political opportunism. There is no reason I can see, therefore, and I would be only too happy if the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) or some member of the government would explain to me where my thinking is wrong, why there must be such haste in acting on this matter.
It could be allowed to sit for a while or referred to a committee. Let everyone have a full opportunity to discuss it. Let us have the various groups throughout the country appear before the committee if they so desire. Let us take it slowly, by stages, and make sure that there is no suggestion of political partisanship. Let us make sure that every faction has its feelings satisfied, to this extent at least, that it has had a full, fair and impartial hearing. There is no injustice that rankles so much as that which results from a feeling that the right to be heard has been denied. There is no punishment meted out in the courts which causes people to become hardened criminals more quickly than the suggestion that they have been denied a fair hearing. I submit that any member who wants a new flag, who wants to do away completely with any suggestion of our present flag and substitute another, must support that line of reasoning.
I resent the suggestion that those of us who prefer the red ensign are just stalling. I am not standing here speaking in the hope that I will put off the evil day, Mr. Speaker. Certainly, when I say that I prefer the red ensign I am aware of the fact that if an election were called my preference would not be shared by a majority of Canadians. There are some who would not want the red ensign in its present form. I am quite willing to go along with a change in that regard. I hope if there is going to be a change in our national flag that change would not be so drastic as to erase all the symbols that I should like to see on our flag to indicate our heritage. However, Mr. Speaker, I will accept that if it is the wish of the people. I do not believe I am so different from those people I represent who would resent not having their voice heard. I will even put up with taking away the red ensign. I will put up with taking away any symbols of our past.
I would even put up with the proposed flag, provided it resulted from the choice of the majority of the people of this country and 
provided it were brought about in a manner that would satisfy all sections of the populace. I would put up with it if all reasonable designs and reasonable suggestions were considered and if parliament was striving its utmost to keep politics out of it.
If this new flag were arrived at in such a way that it would be obvious from the manner in which this house handled it that all these considerations had been taken care of, and that once the new flag had been adopted it would serve to unify the country, then I could accept it. It should of course show respect for history and for the future of our country. I hope I am not being too repetitious, but I have said in this house before that what a new flag is most likely to stand for, if it is a complete departure from the old one, is a feeling of the manner, the method and the time at which it was introduced. I suggested that had there been a national catastrophe and had we changed governments and a flag had been introduced at that time, then most people would, for some time to come at least, associate the new flag with that national catastrophe. I have suggested before that when there is no previous association with the design that is being offered on the flag, then it becomes of importance to see that the method by which it is introduced evokes only happy memories, memories of respect by one part of the country for another.
I have perhaps dwelt long enough, Mr. Speaker, on the method by which a flag is selected. We are speaking on the subamendment now, on the questions that should be put in a referendum. I should like to deal rather briefly with the questions on the referendum; however, I see it is now six o'clock.

subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED UNDER ADJOURNMENT MOTION
SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED UNDER ADJOURNMENT MOTION
speechtext:
Pursuant to the provisions of standing order 3 9A, it is my duty to inform the house that questions to be raised at 10.30 are as follows:
The hon. member for Lake St. John (Mr. Lessard):

Agriculture-feed grain for eastern Canada [Text]
At six o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at 8 p.m.

The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Pearson:
That the government be authorized to take such steps as may be necessary to establish officially as the flag of Canada a flag embodying the emblem proclaimed by His Majesty King George V on November 21, 1921-three maple leaves conjoined on one stem-in the colours red and white then designated for Canada, the red leaves occupying a field of white between vertical sections of blue on the edges of the flag.
And the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Diefenbaker, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. More.
Carried.

Mr. Speaker, I really appreciate those voices shouting "carried, carried" before you called order. I am sure they were referring to the remarks I made when we adjourned at supper time. It is my fervent hope that they have now seen reason, and they are suggesting to me that the trained seals on the government back benches are now going to recant and reflect the views of their constituencies and the responsible views of a member of parliament, instead of following the views of those members of the Liberal party who think in terms of the adhesion or cohesion of the Liberal party rather than the serious question affecting the house in this debate.
I think at six o'clock I had just mentioned the subamendment, the matter of the national referendum or plebiscite, and the questions which should appear in that referendum. I should say at the outset that I am not in entire agreement with the subamendment and I cannot really understand the form in which it is presented. In this subamendment on the question of a national flag as it should be put to the people of Canada we have the red ensign as it is, and the red ensign as it might be amended with some relationship to other ethnic groups in our country. Then we also have that peculiar monstrosity presented to the house by the government as a projected flag, and we also have a one maple leaf design.
I want to make it clear at the outset that I am not at all averse to a national referendum in which people may have a broad choice, but I am totally unable to accept the
Canadian Flag
proposition that in that national referendum this Pearson pennant, as we have known the three maple leaf design proposed by the government, should take equal precedence with the flag that has been so proudly Canada's for 100 years. To me this is preposterous, and I would not be so vehement about it unless it had failed in every requisite that one would think of in connection with a national flag.
It has not been arrived at by any process that the people of this country would like to think would be associated with a flag that represents them. It does not represent the people of this country. It was brought in as a political manoeuvre, presented in that manner and sustained only in any sense of the word because of the political implications behind it. To suggest a national referendum, where that sort of a pennant would take equal precedence with the flag that is so revered and treasured by such a large percentage of the people in this country, is to me just out of keeping with our responsibilities to this country.
I may say that if that flag had anything about it that is artistically pleasing, perhaps I would find some excuse. If I thought that as other than a political gimmick it was attractive even to the members from Quebec,
I might not resent it so much. But, Mr. Speaker, I cannot forget the spectacle of the members of the Creditiste group coming into the house one day, each of them with a little pennant on his desk. That was the flag referred to earlier today by one of my colleagues, red and white with a green maple leaf, divided diagonally between red and white. I must say I do not pretend to be an artist. In this, as in other respects, I am an ordinary citizen of my community where art is concerned; but to me, if we are going to have a flag which is not everything a flag should represent, then at least it should have the advantage of having a pleasing appearance.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) took the trouble on behalf of a group in his constituency-I believe the sons of Norway, who are plugging that same flag-to bring a copy of it around to every member of the house, and I will say it had the distinction of being very attractive. It was not a muddied up or muddled up flag such as that which the government suggests.
I would say, Mr. Speaker, that there is not a man, woman or child in this country who would not like our flag to be at least, if not beautiful, then presentable. This cannot be

Canadian Flag
said for the three leafed monstrosity that this unartistic government presents to us. If I, in pursuance of the question of what should be in the referendum to be submitted to the people, can describe the so-called Pearson pennant, as I am sure it is known across the country, I would say the first thing it brings to mind is a presently noted song. Perhaps it is not too respectable but it deals with the subject of General Jubilation T. Cornpone. I think it is a take-off of a Li'l Abner character, a general who fought all the famous battles, described as Cornpone's anguish, Cornpone's humiliation, Cornpone's defeat, Cornpone's disgrace and Cornpone's retreat. If the government is really suggesting, or if any member of the house wants to put that pennant on a national referendum on the same basis as our revered red ensign, I can only say that I think my reaction will not be too different from that of so many people in this country who listen to the radio or television occasionally and who have some imagination.
To me, this proposed flag with a blue border at each end and three red maple leaves in the centre on a white background sounds like an emblem of that great general, Jubilation T. Cornpone about whom the song was written. The Canadian public cannot be blamed for associating this proposed flag with the political record of the Liberal party. The first blue bar represents the first disgrace which the party suffered-the 60 days of decision. Then, in keeping with General Cornpone's military career, which was a complete failure, we come to Cornpone's humiliation. The first little red maple leaf represents that famous budget-the budget which was put forward and subsequently revised. I am sure this is what is going through the minds of the people of Canada when they look at this pennant. The second maple leaf represents something else-the much heralded pension plan. I am sure all members have heard about Cornpone's defeat. I have in mind the first time this pension plan was brought in, and the manner in which it was presented. The government said: You will take this plan because we presented it; it must be the greatest. The Liberals presented this flag resolution in the same way, though you would never know it today. I can see how the people of Canada will associate the proposed pennant with these events.
General Cornpone, as we all know, had a famous retreat. Talking about a retreat, what happened to the redistribution bill? The Liberals had a great idea. A member of the New

Democratic party suggested a slight amendment. The Liberals went along because the N.D.P. wanted it. Then they found the official opposition would have no part of it. Where is the redistribution bill now? We had thought, from some of the opinions expressed in this house, that the Liberals had really wanted to correct some of the anomalies in the representation of constituencies in this House of Commons. Where is the bill now? Cornpone's retreat.
If this flag were ever accepted by Canada, the last blue bar would represent the most shameful thing of all. It would represent the division caused in this country by the political machinations of the present government in treating as a mere political tool something which is sacred to so many people. What colour is the background to all this? It is the white background of surrender-the surrender of every ideal known to members of this house on the altar of political expediency. Yet members across the way want us to accept this design and consider it in our minds on the same basis as the red ensign, which has represented everything in Canada which we think is worth fighting for and worth retaining.
I suggest the first sign of sense shown in connection with this whole debate is that the Prime Minister is now prepared to consider another course of action. I cannot understand why the right hon. gentleman does not do his thinking before he acts. We in this house have seen so many reversals, so many somersaults, so many withdrawals of ideas, that the one question in the mind of each one of us and of people right across the country is: Why in heaven's name, don't they think a little before bringing these things forward?
When the Prime Minister first introduced this resolution he had in mind that there would be a free vote. The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Watson) has put the evidence on record. It was only after the right hon. gentleman's political henchman got to him that he changed his mind. These men, working behind the scenes, said: Look, this is how we can win so many votes from this group or that. So he changed his mind and some days later he said the government would stand or fall on the resolution. Now, after all this time, the Prime Minister has found that the people are asking: Why should the flag issue have priority? Is it not worth a close, careful and even lengthy scrutiny by parliament? Does the government have no legislation which is urgent or important and which needs to be discussed? These are the questions

being asked in the country. The people have asked them long enough and hard enough for the message finally to sink through to the Prime Minister, and he has retreated to the position which, I submit, he should have taken in the first place.
I believe that when he first introduced this legislation the Prime Minister really believed that it should not be a party matter. Those of us in this house who are aware of the right hon. gentleman's record have never considered him to be a politician, first. I have never considered him to be a statesman, but at least he was a diplomat. As a man who in diplomatic negotiations had to put Canada first, his first thought when he brought in this resolution was for the good of Canada. Then the Liberal politicians got to him. We all know the Liberal politicians. They are people who can sell a lie ten times as fast as a Liberal can tell the truth. They are afraid of the truth because they might not be able to sell it. But I think the truth has finally sunk into the mind of the Prime Minister and even into the minds of those tremendous politicians who belong to his cabinet. They have finally come to realize that to play politics with a symbol such as our national flag, even though it means different things to different groups, is dividing this nation and causing such rifts-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I regret to interrupt the hon. member, but his time has expired.

I realize that it is my duty to speak for the second time on the Canadian flag. The first time I spoke on the subject was on May 28, 1963, during the debate on the address.
Before I begin to speak on this resolution or, rather, on the subamendment, I think I might draw attention to what my dictionary has to say regarding the definition of the word "flag". It says: "A piece of cloth of bunting upon which, usually, some device is placed, used as a standard or ensign". But to me, Mr. Speaker, the important question is not so much what a flag looks like but what it stands for; what it stood for in the past and what it will stand for in the future.
Hear, hear.

I am speaking from personal experience in this regard. I may be the only member in this house who has lived under the hammer and sickle, and I know what this flag stood for and what it will stand for in the future. I also realized before I came to
Canadian Flag
Canada some 35 years ago what the Canadian flag stood for. But much more important to me was what it would stand for in the future. I raised a family, and I know what some of these young people had to go through in countries where freedom is not interpreted in the same way that we interpret it here. I am referring to countries in which schools were used to indoctrinate young people with communistic ideas, with nazi ideas. You can understand, Mr. Speaker, what this flag meant to me and what it still means to me. You will understand how I feel when, as a parent, I see the union jack flying over a school. I and parents like me know this will not be a school in which our children will be indoctrinated with these ideas; that this is a school in which freedom is taught and where freedom means something.
It is not my only duty, Mr. Speaker, to tell you what I had to go through and what this flag means to me; but as the member representing the riding of Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale it is also my duty to speak on behalf of my constituents. I would be remiss in my duty if I did not follow their advice and put forward representations on their behalf. I have received many letters on this question. The resolution which was introduced by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), which was responsible for my receiving these letters, reads as follows:
That the government be authorized to take such steps as may be necessary to establish officially as the flag of Canada a flag embodying the emblem proclaimed by His Majesty King George V on November 21, 1921-three maple leaves conjoined on one stem-in the colours red and white then designated for Canada, the red leaves occupying a field of white between vertical sections of blue on the edges of the flag; and on the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Diefenbaker, and on the amendment to the amendment of Mr. More.
I would like to read some of the letters I have received from my constituents, and in particular from Legions in my area.
Dispense.

I received a telegram from the Sylvania Legion which says:
The Sylvania branch No. 54 of the Canadian Legion goes on record favouring the red ensign as the official flag of Canada.
As I say, Mr. Speaker, I would be remiss in my duty if I did not act on behalf of the people in my riding, after they have elected me three times, and bring their views before the attention of the house and this government. I also received a letter from the Leroy and Melfort branch of the Canadian Legion stating that they were in favour of

Canadian Flag
retaining the red ensign as our national flag. I could go on and on in this respect; there have been similar letters from other branches of the Legion. As I said in my previous speech on this subject, the Prime Minister has introduced this new design that is not one of which the people of Canada will approve. I have received many, many letters and many telegrams to this effect from various organizations. At the time when there was not a member representing Saskatoon one lady asked me to put forward her view and the view of her group that the red ensign should be retained as the Canadian flag.
Why should there be a new Canadian flag, Mr. Speaker? Why should this new design have been introduced in the way it was? Why was it not declared during the election campaign that a new . Canadian flag would be introduced into parliament? I and my opponents had many joint meetings. At those meetings not one of my opponents mentioned that the Liberal party intended to put before parliament a new Canadian flag. Certainly some time after the election it was said that their Prime Minister had stated that within two years a Canadian flag would be approved; but so many of these Liberal promises were made during the election campaign and we have heard nothing more about them since this government took office. If these other promises cannot be kept, why is this flag resolution so necessary? However, Mr. Speaker, believing in democracy as I do, I think there are ways and means of arriving at a solution in respect of our flag. As I say, a flag is not just a bunting; it represents much more than that.
If the house agrees, a compromise could be made. There could be set up a committee composed of representatives of all parties. However, I would be opposed to this if the committee were instructed to discuss only the flag introduced by the Prime Minister, because if this were the case that flag would be nothing but a political flag; nor would I like to see any other flag introduced by the government. The committee should be empowered to recommend a flag and have it approved by the house. Mention was made of a 15-man committee. The composition of the committee was also mentioned as being seven from the Liberal party, five from the official opposition, and one each from the other opposition parties. I think that the report or recommendation from the committee to the house should not be that of just a majority of the committee, but it should be approved by the house. There is nothing unusual about

such a committee. We have a similar situation at the United Nations, where the Russians have the power of veto which they requested. The reason for this is that the rest of the members of the United Nations are democratic or more or less democratic couretries, while Russia is a communist country, and if any question was decided by a majority vote, there is no question about it that the Russian government would lose out every time.
Mr. Speaker, I am very sincere, as I am sure are other members who have spoken before me, when I suggest that the resolution presently before the house involves a political issue. I think the flag issue should be taken out of this chamber and referred to a parliamentary committee, which may come to a conclusion in respect of a Canadian national flag which can no longer be called or referred to as the flag of the Liberal party, a flag of the Conservative party, a flag of the N.D.P. or a flag of the Social Credit party. I am sure most members will agree that a decision made by an all-party committee will not be considered as a decision of a political nature.
Mr. Speaker, I have not been home since the resolution now before us was presented to the house, but I do know the tenor of thought in my constituency. I have received a great number of letters expressing a desire to retain the red ensign rather than to adopt the flag proposed by this government. The general trend of expression in these letters is in favour of this issue being decided by referendum. I have received several letters from people who live in my own home town, which express a desire for me to return and report on the progress of this flag debate. Many of these letters have perhaps been precipitated by the reading of the copies of Hansard I have sent to my constituents. They have asked me to explain the lack of speeches made by members of political parties other than Conservative, and have expressed some astonishment at the absence of speeches of Liberal members. I agree with this opinion and suggest that those on the opposite side of this house should stand in their places and either support the flag proposed by the government or express a contrary point of view. I must report to all hon. members that my constituents do not appreciate the attitude adopted by those members in favour of the proposed design who pretend by acquiescence to be in favour of that flag. I suggest that they should stand and be heard.

Mr. Speaker, in reference to the subamendment, I suggest that if the committee proposed therein cannot come to something approximating a unanimous decision, the national flag for Canada should be decided by plebiscite. Such a plebiscite should include questions similar to those proposed by the subamendment. I would certainly like to see these two questions proposed on any plebiscite: Are you in favour of the Canadian red ensign? Are you in favour of a distinctively Canadian flag embodying the three maple leaf design?
Yes.

I know you all say "yes", but why do you not get up on your feet and take part in this debate?
Mr. Speaker, perhaps a third question should be included in a plebiscite to this effect: Are you in favour of a distinctive Canadian flag? I think those three questions should be included in any plebiscite presented to the people.
I am very disappointed that in Canada today there is a question being raised about a change in the Canadian flag. Thousands and thousands, and perhaps millions of Canadians have come to Canada from foreign lands. Many of these people realize that the countries which they left adopted ensigns other than those of tradition, such as the swastika, but were left with something emblematic of a dictatorial power. Flags such as the red ensign have great histories. Our soldiers have fought several wars under the red ensign. To ignore the requests of these veterans to retain it, and that which is symbolized by it, is to ignore the sympathies of the majority of Canadians. I think the sympathies of these people who have fought in wars on behalf of Canada should be given full and thorough consideration.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to refer to one very short letter I received from a South African war veteran. This man is not one of my constituents but lives in the province of British Columbia and has not authorized me to disclose his name. He is a very outspoken gentleman and has said that when he enlisted as a young man for service in the South African war he did so under the emblem of Canada. He has lived his life since in Canada under the red ensign, and he states that in his senior years his heart bleeds at any suggestion that Canada abandon the red ensign as its national flag.
Mr. Speaker, I could spend another 30 minutes reading portions of letters and telegrams I have received from individuals who
Canadian Flag
wish to voice an opinion in respect of any flag to be adopted by Canada. However, in conclusion I must state that I think it is my privilege and duty, as it is of every other member of parliament, to stand up in this chamber and express the views of the people I represent in respect of the retention of the Canadian red ensign. In spite of my own feelings, I think those members of this House of Commons who favour the three maple leaf flag design, or any other design, should stand up and express that feeling. These members were not sent to parliament to remain in their seats, silent, but to take part in debates of this kind, whether emotionally charged or not.
Thank you, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to take part in this debate because it involves something that affects every Canadian citizen. It involves a subject which every Canadian should have the right to discuss, and concerning which he should express an opinion. In view of the dissension between the two founding races, this matter should be allowed to remain in abeyance until the emotional factor has died down. Once the flag resolution has been voted on the matter will be over and done with, and if careful planning and consideration is not given to both points of view, the ties that have bound these two peoples so closely may be broken for all time.
Mr. Speaker, in speaking on the subamendment moved by the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. More) I must say I am in favour, because I feel it outlines the proper procedure to be followed in respect of an issue such as this. If at the outset the flag issue had been introduced to this house in such a way as suggested by the subamendment, I am sure emotionalism would have been absent from the debate.
Before continuing I should like to say that I support the red ensign, I am sure I speak for the majority of my constituents, who represent every nationality in the world and live in perfect harmony. These people set an example to be followed by people all over the world.
Many people of Ukrainian origin live in my constituency, and I cannot agree more with the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr), than when he stated that he came from people who believe in tradition and do not throw tradition out the window when it has served its usefulness. These people respect the traditions of people of other nationalities. They feel strongly about the union jack and red ensign.

Canadian Flag
These people are proud and hardy people who were not afraid to settle in some of the remote areas of our country. These are the people who, when the chips are down, were not afraid to answer their adopted country's call. The same can be said, Mr. Speaker, for Ukrainians, the Rumanians, the Dutch, the Germans, the Scandinavians, the Polish, the Russians, people from Greece and France, in fact, all these people from wherever they came. This country was the country of their choice, a land of freedom, a land of opportunity.
Again, we have the Doukhobors of Russian origin who, I am proud to say, are my neighbours at home and who, because of their religious beliefs and their refusal to bear arms, were persecuted in their own land under the Czarist regime. They came to this country and found their way of life, of toil and peace. These people are the people who today, sir, are some of the best farmers, lawyers, doctors, teachers and engineers. They have excelled in any profession they chose and they were able to achieve this under our flag. Do you think these people would want to see the Christian crosses stripped from our flag? The same can be said for the other minority groups who have also played their part in the development of this country.
People of every nationality have developed our country and have had some part in our heritage. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, can you honestly see the fairness in taking away from a majority in order to satisfy a minority?
We talk about the two founding races. What about our Indian people who were forgotten by the Liberal government? It took the Conservative government under the leadership of the present Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) to give them some of the recognition they deserved-representation in the Senate, the franchise, the right to better education and better housing. These people were not a bit backward in answering their country's call in time of need, and the ones I have talked to are in favour of the red ensign.
This three maple leaves flag design is the choice of the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), a Prime Minister who is the leader of a minority party and who acts like he was the leader of a party with a great majority, a man who was a Nobel peace prize winner and who is now acting like a dictator. He has said: This is my design, my flag, the one you will accept or face an election. Of course, Mr. Speaker, the thought of an election struck fear into the Liberal party, with their many unfulfilled promises of the 1963 campaign when the flag

was hardly mentioned; and of course this also shook some of the members of the other three parties so that many of them jumped into line.
How about the way this flag was chosen? I read that the Prime Minister had invited a group of reporters to his home and when they arrived they found the Prime Minister waiting for them and nursing a scotch and soda. Drinks and sandwiches were then served. I am not a drinking man and maybe this flag looks better after you have had a few drinks. Maybe some of my hon. friends opposite have viewed it in that light. Finally, after looking at many designs, the Prime Minister picked up the flag with the three maple leaves and said, "This is it, this is my design", just like a president of a company calling in his salesmen, introducing a new product to them and saying: Here it is, get out and sell it. I will not say whether they all did but some have tried, I think without too much success. So some reporters have turned on the Conservative party and have blamed them for carrying on a filibuster, which we all know could not be further from the truth.
If the Prime Minister and the group he leads-apparently it is not a party any more- are afraid to let the people of Canada speak out for themselves on this issue, then I am going to speak out for what I am sure the majority of my constituents want, and I do not care whether it takes four days, four weeks or four months. Twice in a generation men were prepared to give four years of their blood and sweat, and in many cases their lives, in order to fight for the freedom for which our flag stands. Then the Prime Minister goes to Winnipeg as a guest speaker at the Royal Canadian Legion convention and unfurls his three maple leaves flag design. What alternative did those Legion members have but to boo and heckle this so-called flag? This was the only way they could show their disapproval of his choice.
Unlike some members I did not send out a questionnaire to my constituents but I did receive many letters, all of them supporting the red ensign, not one supporting the Pearson political pennant. When the hon. member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan) referred to the Liberal campaign literature containing their election promises, there was no mention made of the flag. Why was this contentious issue dragged into this session like a cat being dragged backwards by the tail? Was it to cover up for all the other legislation that was not ready, for instance, the Canada pension plan, the legislation based on the report of

the MacPherson royal commission on transportation and the legislation to assist Canadian magazines based on the O'Leary report, just to mention a tew?
During the last campaign, meetings were held with all the different party representatives present. I do not think my Liberal opponent mentioned the flag but he did talk about $2 a bushel for No. 1 northern wheat and $3 a bushel for the first 300 bushel unit. He talked about two ministers of agriculture, one for eastern Canada and one for western Canada. This was also promised by the Prime Minister when he was campaigning in the prairie provinces. I do not know what he said in British Columbia but apparently from what we have heard from the other side of the house and from the Postmaster General (Mr. Nicholson) regarding the Fraserview homes for veterans, it is fine to make promises when you are in opposition but you should not be expected to carry them out when your party is elected as a government and you are a minister of the crown. I would not think my Liberal opponent in the last election would walk into any of the Legion branches in my constituency and say, "I think we will take down the red ensign and replace it with the three maple leaves flag".
Look at the way the flag issue has been introduced. Is this the action of a man who cares? I think not, Mr. Speaker. Instead it is the action of a dictatorial prime minister, an arrogant, bureaucratic and careless government. After all, there are 10 provinces in Canada, so why not call a meeting of the representatives of the provinces and have them decide on a design they could all accept instead of having some of them flying the red ensign, some the union jack and others flying something else?
I do not have to tell hon. members that people are becoming very flag conscious these days. When I was home I attended fairs in my constituency. I could not help but notice that in the parades practically every float had a flag, some of them four or five, and I did not see one Pearson flag. The flags were the red ensign and the union jack. I think people are beginning to realize that something is going to be taken away from them. In western Canada we are not flag wavers but we do believe in what our flag stands for and nobody is going to take that away.
People have talked about the blood that flows in their veins in this house. I will tell you the kind of blood that flows in my veins. It is Irish on both sides, and if the Prime Minister thinks he is going to ram this flag 20220-459
Canadian Flag
down my throat he has got another think coming. When I went home in the early part of June at the time the flag issue was first mentioned people said to me: What is the matter with you members? You are getting $18,000 a year and you are wasting time discussing the flag. Have you not got something better to discuss? But when I told them what it was all about they changed and said: Do not let them take our flag.
Carried.

Why do hon. members over there not get up and speak?
There was only one man, the hon. member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan), who had the courage to stand up yesterday and say where he stood. I do not believe his constituency is too much different from some of the others in Toronto. I would say to some hon. members opposite, "Enjoy yourselves, because it is later than you think." Why do not hon. members opposite want to let this question go to the people? If they are so sure they are right and the majority of the people are with them, let the question go to the people. If the people decide that this is the flag they want, then that is fine; I will accept it. However, I will never accept the manner in which the Prime Minister is attempting to ram this flag through this house.
I should like to refer to the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Dupuis)-that is a good portfolio for him, because I never heard him say anything in this house. I want to tell him that they are going to be looking for Liberal candidates in my constituency. He can come out there to run and bring his 100,000 flag stickers-
Do you want some?

-that will assure my re-election.
No, Mr. Speaker, I will tell you what hon. members opposite would like. I can say that my remarks are going to affect some members in the third, fourth and fifth parties. They would have liked to have shoved this flag question through quietly, then have a recess. They could have gone away for a couple of months and come back smiling and tanned, hoping the people had forgiven and forgotten. I do not believe it is going to work that way.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would again suggest that this issue should be referred to a committee, as has been suggested, in order that a design may be brought forward which

Canadian Flag
would be acceptable to all. I hope that it would be a design that would unite and not divide.

Mr. Speaker, I do not suppose there is any other member in this house or at least not very many of the members in this house, who have caused you as little bother as I have. I do not speak very often in the house. I have been here longer than most of you, and I always thought I could learn a lot more by sitting in my seat and listening to others than by talking. I have learned all I know by listening to others. I did not rise very quickly a few minutes ago because I was expecting perhaps we would get a speech from the other side of the house. I would be content to sit down and let anybody speak in my place. As a matter of fact, the only reason I am taking part in this debate is because of the fact I represent a riding that has instructed me to speak for it.
I have received a lot of mail, but I am not going to bother reading it to you. I received a lot a petitions signed by hundreds of people who favour the red ensign. I am speaking tonight because I favour the red ensign and I believe at least three quarters of the people in Canada favour the red ensign. Why the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) insists on making us take this flag, regardless of whether or not we want it, is more than I can understand. The Prime Minister was appointed- he was not elected, he was appointed by the Governor General-to the highest position any man in Canada can hold. As such, he is supposed to be a statesman. He cannot run Canada with one province; he has to have support from all the provinces of this country. I cannot understand anyone who would offer us a flag without giving us a choice. Then he said that there would not be a free vote and if we voted against the flag there would be an election. I, for one, would welcome an election on the flag issue. However, I would not welcome it in so far as the unity of the country is concerned because it would split the country wide open.
I have been here for a long time. I have never quarrelled with anybody. I have been able to get along with the French, the same as I do with the English. I have a French community in my riding. I never got one letter from those fellows, and they are fine fellows, just as good as any others in my riding. I never got one letter from the French in my riding insisting on this new flag. I have received a lot of letters from the people in my riding and with the exception of two,

all those letters favour the red ensign. The two letters did not oppose the red ensign but wanted something added to it. As I said before, I am a red ensign man. I do not want to say anything tonight that will offend anybody else. I do not think that is the way we should go about this matter. There has been enough acrimony in this debate, and I do not want to add any more. We have been able to get along in this country for years without quarrelling, so surely in this enlightened day and age we will be able to get along for the next hundred years without having any interruption.
I was rather surprised when the leader of the separatists at the other end of this room said one day that he would welcome a revolution in Quebec. I think that was a terrible thing to say.
Who said that?

The leader of the Creditistes at the other end of the room. I heard him say it because I was in the house when he said it. I think that is a terrible thing to say. Whenever there has been a revolution in another country, there has been a lot of bloodshed. If that is what you want, a lot of bloodshed, well I understand a lot of blood was spilled over this carpet yesterday when I was not here. We cannot stir people up emotionally, and this is an emotional issue, so the best thing to do is to be careful of what you say. You should not stir up somebody else who may be more emotional than you are yourself. I am one of those whose temper can be aroused, too, but I do not like to quarrel with anybody. I like to get along with people. I think the fact I have been here for so many years is the result of my ability to get along with men, and women too, for that matter.
Explain.

I have often said that I never saw a horse that I could not drive. A horse is not much different from a man, and there are some of them to whom you have to give a good licking in order to get along with them. There are some men you cannot get along with either, unless you give them a good licking. I believe in the old style; I believe in cracking down on a man who won't mind his own business. I believe that very often the old laws we had years and years ago are more effective than the laws they have now.
However, I do not intend to take too much of the time of the house tonight. The last

speaker brought out many of the points I intended to bring out, so I do not intend to repeat them. The hon. lady member from Northumberland (Miss Jewett)-I do not see her in the house at the moment-made a statement when she was speaking on the flag issue two or three weeks ago. She said that she was appealing to fellow M.P.'s to disregard their own personal preference for a flag, and also the feeling of their constituencies about a flag which would best serve Canada. I was elected a member of parliament for a certain area and I intend to speak for the people in that area. When it comes to the point where I cannot speak for them they can replace me with someone else, and that is exactly what will happen. You know, Mr. Speaker, you can pick the best man in any community but you do not know what you have got until after you have got him. You do not know what his reactions will be until after he is elected a member of parliament.
Some people come here thinking they are some special creation and they forget all about their constituencies, but those people do not stay here for long, and during my time I have seen a lot of them leave. Mind you, they were a lot smarter men then I and could make wonderful speeches, but when it came down to solid facts they forgot all about the people who elected them. They did not pay any attention to their mail. I have seen fellows with mail piled a foot deep on their desks and who thought all they had to do was get up in the house and make a speech. More people talked themselves out of this house than talked themselves into it, and I would suggest to the younger members of the house that if you want to stay here, don't talk too often and then they don't know how stupid you are. That is the reason why I have stayed here so long.
When this flag issue first came up I thought the Prime Minister would at least give us a choice. I am sure hundreds of designs were submitted to him, as they were to all of us, but in my opinion he picked the one that was the least attractive. Had he gone to the Indians or Eskimos I am sure he would have found an artist among them who could have drawn a better flag than he produced.
I do not understand why the Prime Minister will not accept the amendment proposed by the Leader of the Opposition. This is the best way out that I know for him, and he should let the people tell him what flag they want. I myself do not want any particular flag. If the majority of the people want another 20220-459i
Canadian Flag
