flag I will go along with that, but I do object to having no choice whatsoever and I cannot understand this attitude of the Prime Minister and why he has been so ill-advised.
During the time the Liberals were in opposition they had two members who had more to say than anybody else, and knew how to run the country, or at least they said so, when the Conservatives were in power. Now they are in the cabinet, and if this is the advice they have given the Prime Minister, all I can say is that it is not very good advice.
I suggest that he take advice from some of his backbenchers who have more sense about flags than he himself has.
I have a daughter-in-law who is a Ukrainian. Her family has been in this country for a generation and she can speak Ukrainian. She has a family of four, the youngest being about nine, but she has never tried to teach her children to speak Ukrainian. These people were satisfied to come to Canada and live like Canadians. In fact all the different nationalities that have come here in the last 25 years do not clamour for us to speak their languages. They are good people, fine people, and have contributed a lot to this country, but they do not demand that their languages be spoken, and why a minority language should be forced on the rest of Canada is more than I can understand.
I do not think the Prime Minister can stay prime minister unless he is ready and willing to do the things that the ten provinces want him to do. The sooner he gets that into his head the better he will get along. If he is the statesmen he should be, he will not listen to any minority group and do the things they want him to do. He does not have to do those things, and he does not have to be embarrassed about it either. At present he is embarrassing his own members who are trying their best to follow him against their will. I will not disclose any names, but some of them have told me they do not want to go along with the Prime Minister but what else can they do when he says, "Either vote for my flag or else there will be an election"? Like a great many others they do not want an election and I do not believe the country wants an election.
Surely to goodness there is not any group who would want a flag which the majority of the Canadian people would not accept? I hope the Prime Minister will take this advice from me. I have been here longer than he has. I do not pretend to know as much as he does, but surely I could not have stayed here for this length of time without being able to

Canadian Flag
figure out the best thing to do. I have been in some pretty good fights since I came here, and I say to the Prime Minister that the easiest way to work this thing out is not to quarrel about it but to talk it out, and talk sensibly to each other.
I hope I have not said anything that has offended anybody in the house because I did not get up for that purpose. I would not want to offend anybody; I like my friends too well for that. I like my people at home, and I had to get up and say something about the flag because this is the flag they want, and so long as they want it I am satisfied to speak for them. If we cannot get it, then I hope to goodness we can appoint a joint committee of the house and the Senate to go into the question and bring back a recommendation. If there is an overwhelming majority of the committee in favour of that recommendation then I would say accept it, and it does not have to be a unanimous recommendation. I do not think it would be possible to achieve that, but it should be a great majority before we accept anything.
The Prime Minister has said he will allow a free vote, but now that so much time has elapsed I am afraid a free vote would not count as much as it would have a month ago. He should take a second look at this matter. I believe he acted like a school teacher when he said, "Either you pass this flag or you don't get any summer holiday." You cannot talk to grown men like that. I was whip of this party when we had 208 members to handle. I got along fine with them and from my experience I can tell you that you cannot tell grown men what they have to do. They know what they have to do without anybody telling them. You can ask them to do something, but you cannot tell them.
I hope the Prime Minister will come to his senses before he has destroyed the unity of Canada. If we are to have unity in Canada it has to be unity in ten provinces, not in nine, or one. We have to be all united and the sooner we are all united and go ahead with something more important than the flag, the better it will be for Canada. If the government has any legislation that is more important than the flag, why does it not introduce it? Why does it put the flag ahead of important legislation? Nobody told the government to bring in the flag and nobody insisted on its being introduced. Because we are talking to stop the government from passing this flag, and this is the only hope we have of stopping it, the Prime Minister thinks this is a filibuster. This is not a filibuster. This is a question which, once it is

settled, is settled for all time. The decision, once taken, cannot be altered. I hope the Prime Minister-and this is all I intend to say-
Hear, hear.

Now listen, boys, and learn a little more. I could stand here and speak for a long time. I have plenty of notes I have not looked at yet. Nobody else has seen them; I wrote them myself. But I do not like reading notes, even though in this particular debate I would prefer to have used my notes so as to avoid the possibility of my saying something which, later, I would find I had not really intended to say; sometimes we are led away on such occasions as this into saying things we might afterwards regret. On this occasion, let me remind hon. members opposite, I could go on for another half hour, at least. I do not know how much time I have left to me, but I have not been called to order yet and I wish to thank the Chair very much.

Mr. Speaker,
I would be delighted to take the wise advice of my hon. friend from Huron (Mr. Cardiff) and sit still and learn a little more; but as this debate progresses and the month of August draws to a close I find it difficult to stand up in this chamber without indulging in a little reminiscing.
The minds of many of us on this side of the house, when we think of the many trouble spots in the world today, turn to an occasion almost 25 years ago, when we had to stand up and make decisions-decisions which, once reached, could not be treated lightly. In September, 1939, many of us, with little or no idea of what the future held, decided that Canada was worth fighting for and that our way of life should be retained, never of course thinking for one minute that the symbols which we cherished then would have to be surrendered on the altar of political expediency.
When the original resolution was introduced, it appeared, because of the heavy propaganda with which it was launched, that those opposed would be submerged by weight of numbers. But the constructive approach by members of this party has kept debate at a high level. Now it appears across the country that resistance has stiffened and that support for a more democratic choice for a flag design is being registered. It was to this end that the subamendment was introduced, and if it were adopted would show in no uncertain terms the divergency of opinion regarding a national flag.

By supporting this subamendment, the members of this party are being more charitable than were some other members of this house when Bill C-97 was introduced on October 2, 1963, and Bill C-83 on March 25 of this year. On both those occasions attempts were made to prevent first reading of a bill which would adopt by statute the red ensign as Canada's national flag. Because of the action taken with regard to the introduction of these particular bills, I am fully convinced that the people of Canada wish a choice in the design of a national flag. No amount of verbiage on the part of this government can conceal the fact there is bitter resentment not only regarding the design of the Prime Minister's flag but in the method used to secure its adoption. Many views were expressed to me, not all favourable, at a time when the flag issue was not so controversial as it is now. Needless to say, I am now glad their opinions were given at a time more free from emotion and sentiment. However, as I suggested, all submissions were not in favour of the red ensign as it flies today. There were those who suggested modification as defined in the subamendment. In a mood of compromise there have been suggestions that the present flag be retained, with further recognition of Canada's multicultural existence. At least those who feel additions are needed to a truly national flag should at least have the opportunity to put forward their ideas.
Still, it is obvious there are those with strong convictions who are willing to seek some common ground on which to settle this controversial issue. The subamendment introduced by the hon. member from Regina City (Mr. More) is the most sensible device yet suggested to give the people of this country the right to exercise that freedom of choice which is presently being denied them. It is hard to understand in this day and age why a minority government should use such an arbitrary method of forcing on the Canadian people a lacklustre flag, supported by illogical arguments and dedicated to rancour and division.
On the other hand, those who favour the three maple leaf design would have an equal opportunity to vote for the flag of their choice. They would be doing this on an individual basis and should be glad of the opportunity to register their opinions without political pressure or fear of any recriminations. It should be an honour for those who wish to relegate the red ensign to history to stand and be counted in support of a design which appeals to their particular fancy. Those who wish all symbols of our
Canadian Flag
British heritage obliterated from our flag should welcome a plebiscite in which they could favour a design bereft of those emr blems of our Christian civilization. This arboreal mutation of sea and tree is entitled to that recognition which the faithful can promote in a flag combination of wood and water.
If the government feels the Canadian public is overwhelmingly in favour of its design, then of course it is justified in the action being taken, but most indications are to the contrary. The government would immediately acquire considerable respect if even one or two of the suggestions made in this debate were considered.
Surely the suggestions made in the subamendment are not so outrageous as to be ignored completely. Surely reason and compromise are not words so foreign to our vocabulary that they must be disregarded. The official opposition has made it possible to discuss the flag issue in terms of the wishes and desires of all people in Canada, as opposed to the government's hard-headed stand on the three maple leaf design or nothing.
With the submission of literally hundreds of designs there must also be thousands of individuals whose creative imagination might yet produce a flag design acceptable to many people in this country. But under existing conditions there is no incentive or effort to produce anything but hostility.
A great disservice will be effected if the present amendments are ignored and the government proceeds on its present course towards that situation best described as an irresistible force meeting an immovable object. While I am personally in favour of any measure which will ensure Canadian unity and understanding, I cannot easily relinquish my feelings for that flag which has been recognized for a hundred years. The red ensign is a flag of dignity and nobility. It is a proud emblem of a great nation. It inspires pride and confidence in our democratic institutions over which it flies. It is an appropriate mark of our past and a distinguishing figure of our future. Those who have fought under its colours have an abiding pride in the traditions it represents. Those who promote its continuing existence today are remaining true to a trust which will ever be maintained by all who will never yield where principle or honour is concerned.
I have not used any documents in the course of my remarks, or excerpts from newspapers, or letters. However, these only serve

Canadian Flag
to assure me that there is an ever increasing weight of public opinion which is dissatisfied with the method devised to promote the government's flag. Incidentally, Mr. Speaker, the press can be of tremendous value at a time like this by faithful and objective reporting. But regardless of whether or not the voice of reason is heard, there will be no abject surrender on a topic which tears at the very roots of a nation. This is a time to bind and not to cleave, and I trust that methods may yet be found to mend our differences and resolve our difficulties.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. E. Pascoe (Moose Jaw-Lake Centre):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I make no apologies for speaking on the subamendment that is now before us. I consider that it is the responsibility and, if I can be more emphatic, the duty of each member to speak on the flag issue and the move of the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) to take the red ensign from us. After all, as has been explained by many hon. members, the Prime Minister asked us all to express our views. This is not a filibuster. Members of the official opposition are doing what they were elected to do, namely to exert a restraining influence, and if I could be more blunt I might say to block foolish, unwise and unwanted government action. I am one of the majority of Canadians who consider that removal of the Canadian red ensign is unwise, foolish and unwanted. I repeat, this is not a filibuster. We are doing what must be done in an effort to prevent a great mistake that Canadians would have to live with for a long, long time. We are acting responsibly in the public interest, and to a greater and greater extent the public is beginning to appreciate this, in spite of certain biased press reports and certain statements by government leaders.
We are not holding up government legislation, as has been explained by other speakers, because there is no urgent government legislation before us. There should be government action on many pressing problems, but none of this very essential action has been taken, or at least it has not been directed into definite legislation that could be considered by parliament. How can we be accused of holding up government legislation, when the Prime Minister admits that he has nothing more for us to do now but pass his flag? The Prime Minister has told us that if we conclude the flag debate on the terms he has dictated, we can have a recess. I was going to say "a summer recess", Mr. Speaker, but that season is now past. As other speakers have said, we in the official opposition place

our duty and responsibility above the offer of a holiday. By using up our own holiday time we cannot, in any fair way, be accused of holding up government legislation that is not ready for us.
As I have said, Mr. Speaker, each member of this house should make his or her position clear on this very upsetting and emotional flag issue thrust on the country by the Prime Minister. I will make my position clear at the beginning of my remarks. I think the Canadian people should have an opportunity to express their wishes on such a personal and emotional question as a national flag. That is why I am speaking in support of the subamendment. As has been pointed out by other speakers, holding a plebiscite is not a very common practice in our system of democratic government. I agree that this is so. But in this particular matter of choosing a national flag, I think it is essential, in the interest of general acceptance of that flag, that the people be given an opportunity to express their views and thus make the choice by a majority decision. This is all we are asking in the subamendment and the amendment.
This particular flag issue is not an ordinary problem of government policy that can be changed by removing the government at the next election. With an ordinary piece of parliamentary legislation concerning economic or fiscal policy, that can be revised or removed by a succeeding government without too much effect on the public, I do not consider that a plebiscite is necessary. But this flag issue is entirely different. It is an intensely emotional question, and if a flag is chosen it will remain as our national flag and cannot be changed by a succeeding government. That is why we should have a plebiscite.
The subamendment clarifies the amendment moved by our leader proposing such a plebiscite. The Prime Minister and his supporters are opposed to this suggestion of a plebiscite. Why? They say a plebiscite would bring out -and these are their words-divisions in this country and would create new dissensions. The Prime Minister should have thought of this before he decided, apparently all by himself or at least with only a few advisers -or should I say, ill-advisers-to foist his three maple leaf design on Canada.
I am sure-and others have made the same statement-that foisting an ill-considered flag on the people, without their consent by their vote, will create a great deal more division and dissension than could ever be caused by a plebiscite. I firmly believe that the people- at least, those in the area for which I speak-

want to be consulted about the flag; they want to have a hand in making this very important decision, this very emotional decision. I believe the Prime Minister is beginning to realize this at last. I think the great volume of letters he is receiving is having an effect on him. How else can one explain his apparent change of mind, or at least his changed attitude? Now he says he might consider the setting up of a special all-party committee to study the issue and bring in a report. Of course, there are strings to this offer; but at least it appears to be a softening of his earlier dictatorial attitude. If we cannot have a plebiscite, the matter of an all-party committee to study flag designs and bring in a recommendation might be considered.
The members of that committee would have a great responsibility and must be able to represent the views of the majority of their constituents. When and if such a committee is set up, each member should have received over 50 per cent of the votes cast in his constituency in the 1963 federal election. In this way those members would be considered as speaking for the majority of their constituents.
Mr. Speaker, it appears that agreement in respect of such a committee has not been reached. I will now return to the question in respect of the plebiscite. The subamendment moved by the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. More) lists four choices, or questions. The first is in respect of the retention of the Canadian red ensign in its present form. The second relates to the red ensign with changes, emblematic of the main heritages of the two founding races. The third relates to the three maple leaf design, commonly referred to as the Pearson flag. The fourth choice relates to the one maple leaf design.
Mr. Speaker, when I speak in support of the subamendment I am speaking for the many constituents who have written to me. I have received more than 800 letters expressing support for the red ensign. I received my first letter today in favour of the Pearson flag. In addition to those individuals who have written in favour of the red ensign, many have expressed support for a plebiscite. In view of the fact we are considering that subject at this time I should like to quote portions of several letters I have received. I think it is my duty to do so in an attempt to show that I am not speaking merely from a personal feeling, but from the point of view of my constituents.
Canadian Flag
Mr. Speaker, I only intend to read short portions of these letters, and I will name those places from which they emanate.
The first letter was written from Strasbourg and states in part:
We consider it an insult to our intelligence that we have been denied a referendum.
The second letter is from Watrous and states in part:
Regarding the flag. Most of the people that I have spoken with are in favour of the red ensign and those that are lukewarm on the subject at least feel there should be a vote on the matter.
The next letter is from Pense, and states:
-75 per cent-
Referring to this district-
-in favour of having a vote on the matter.
The next letter is from Nokomis and in part states:
Regarding the flag issue-: Everyone I have talked to concerning this issue are of one mind. A vote should have been held asking if a distinctive Canadian flag was desired by the people.
Another letter I received from Strasbourg states:
I don't think Mr. Pearson should be allowed to get away with such high handed tactics in regard to a flag we have had for so long. The people should have a chance to voice their opinion in such an important matter.
I received this letter from Semans, which states:
As for the people around here, whether they are for the red ensign or not, the vast majority feels that a new flag should not be imposed on us without a national referendum. They feel that, if the majority of the Canadian people want a new flag then a new flag it should be, but if the majority want the red ensign then the red ensign should be maintained.
Mr. Speaker, I received a telegram from the Semans, Saskatchewan, branch of the Canadian Legion which was accompanied by four pages of signatures, and which states:
We strongly deplore the arbitrary action of your minority government-
This telegram was sent to Mr. Pearson.
-in dictating to the people that they shall have a new flag. This contravenes the democratic rights of every Canadian. We respectfully urge that the government call a national plebiscite and restore to the people their democratic privileges of deciding whether they want the red ensign or a new flag.
Mr. Speaker, in order to show that the point of view I am presenting is not that held only by the people in my constituency, I should like to refer briefly to statements from other sources. The first is from Toronto in the form

Canadian Flag
of a circular letter which states in the third paragraph:
One way we can be effective is to demand a plebiscite or national vote on the flag issue.
The second quotation I should like to refer to appears in an editorial in the Toronto Telegram of August 2, 1964 and in part states:
The Canadian ensign must not be lowered without the consent of the people.
No decision of the House of Commons, by free vote or otherwise, to strike our historic ensign and replace it with a pennant of the Prime Minister's choosing can be construed as expressing the consensus of the nation.
The voice of the people can be heard, on this issue only through a national plebiscite.
Mr. Speaker, I think that brief reference to this important editorial indicates the whole gist of it and expresses the opinion of the majority of Canadians.
I should now like to quote from an article which appeared in the Victoria Colonist as follows:
-the request to the egocentric Prime Minister to allow the citizens of Canada to vote about the flag.
They were referring to a national plebiscite.
I should like to quote from an article appearing in the Ottawa Citizen of June 29, 1964, after the Prime Minister first introduced this new design to replace the red ensign. This article refers to a poll taken in Winnipeg in respect of the flag issue, and not a flagpole.
Seventy four per cent of those polled favoured a national referendum on the flag.
I should like to now quote from a letter I received from the dominion president of the Canadian corps association. I am sure every member of parliament received a copy of this letter. The president states:
Therefore, the Canadian corps association, dominion command, again emphatically requests the Prime Minister of Canada, and parliament as a whole, to place this subject before the people, at the next regularly scheduled general election. Let the voters finalize this matter.
Mr. Speaker, I hesitate to mention this matter in the House of Commons when the hon. member for Northumberland (Miss Jewett) is not in her seat, but I told her I was going to make reference to the amazing statement she made in which she asked every member to vote in favour of Mr. Pearson's design, disregarding the expressed wishes of their constituents. As I say, I was very amazed at that. I took her to task in an earlier speech and evidently what I said came to the attention of the newspaper in her district. She represents the constituency
[Mr. Pascoe.l
of Northumberland. The editor of the paper there saw my comments and sent me a copy of the Cobourg Sentinel-Star for July 22 last in which is published the results of a poll conducted in her constituency of Northumberland. The headline is "Northumberland wants ensign, favour nation-wide vote, county people are emphatic, decisive choice is made". The report goes on to say that in the survey 626 people were asked for their opinions and the result was considerably more than two to one in favour of the red ensign. With regard to the question of a plebiscite, which we are now considering, the question asked in the poll was: "Do you favour a vote on the issue of a national flag"? The survey showed that 358 favoured a plebiscite, 130 were opposed and the remainder either had no opinion or preferred a plebiscite provided no cost was involved.
As I say, I am sorry the hon. member for Northumberland is not present, but I am sure she received a copy of this newspaper survey. To continue further on the matter of a plebiscite I should like to read an excerpt from an editorial which appeared in The Legionary for July, 1964. I think it should be put on the record. It reads as follows:
The Legionary believes that the flag question is such an issue and again strongly urges the Prime Minister to let the Canadian people decide, one way or another through a national plebiscite. It is the most democratic way of solving this problem. It is the only way to ascertain what the people really want. And the request for a plebiscite is sure to be warmly supported by all Canadians of good will and moderation because, no matter what the result, if the issue were settled by a parliamentary vote only, grave doubts would arise in the minds of a great many citizens that it represented the will of the people. These doubts would linger on for many years and would remain a serious obstacle to the attainment of national unity. So please, Mr. Prime Minister, let the people decide. It would be a statesmanlike solution and might well be a nation saving move.
I think that brief editorial comment certainly sums up the stand we in the opposition are taking. Finally, with regard to the need for a plebiscite I should like to refer to a report which appeared in the Amherst Daily News on December 29, 1961 before the Prime Minister became prime minister. He was being interviewed at a press conference held in Halifax and was being questioned with regard to a flag. He expressed the opinion then that there should be a distinctive flag, and was asked this question:
How would you poll the people on this?
This was his reply:
We would poll the people when we have a general election. And if they don't like the idea of a distinctive Canadian flag which can't be

mistaken for that of any other country, they'll let us know in no uncertain terms.
That was the statement that the present Prime Minister made at a press conference in Halifax on December 29, 1961. I think 1 have put enough quotations on the record to show that the people of my constituency want a plebiscite, and I believe it is just an average constituency that is representative of a great part of Canada. The galleries have been crowded during the flag debate. These daily visitors from all parts of Canada have heard our side of the question, and when I say "our side" I mean the views of members of the official opposition. I have met some of the visitors afterwards and they have expressed surprise at the silence on this question on the government side. I might add that I too am surprised at the silence of government supporters. The gallery visitors and Canadians generally will have to place their own interpretation on the absence of personally expressed opinions in support of the Prime Minister's flag.
I am not a lawyer, Mr. Speaker, but I understand that in court it is recognized legal practice that when the defendant has a poor case he says as little as possible. Perhaps this explains the silence of the government and its supporters. During a period of heckling directed against one of our speakers the Solicitor General (Mr. MacNaught), who is in the house now, was challenged to tell the house why he was supporting the Prime Minister's attempt to remove the Canadian red ensign, which has been our officially recognized flag for so long. His reply was that his vote against the red ensign would be his speech. I do not think Canadians will accept such an offhand attitude. They will want to know why he is voting against our present flag, why he, the Prime Minister and their colleagues are so determined to remove the Canadian red ensign from flagpoles all across Canada.
We would like to hear from more government members. I do not throw out a challenge, because that might be embarrassing to them, but I point out again that the people in the galleries and people all across Canada want to hear their explanations or excuses. The voters want to read in the newspapers or hear on radio or television why government members want to have a flag that severs all connection with our past history. In the hope that at least one of them will rise to defend his intention to vote against the red ensign if we ever come to the vote, I will conclude my remarks by inviting any 20220-460
Canadian Flag
member on the opposite side of the house to rise and defend his position.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in the debate this evening on the subject that is before the house I consider it to be a great privilege as well as a duty on behalf of the historic riding of Lanark which I have the honour to represent. I first wish to express my congratulations to the many members who have taken part in the debate. As a former speaker said this evening, they have distinguished themselves and their speeches have been of a very high calibre. With that I agree, and while I should like to mention all of them, time does not permit.
But, Mr. Speaker, I would be delighted to hear some of the government supporters express their views, especially some of my next door neighbours, and others a little more distant from my riding. I should like to hear my neighbour to the east who represents that great county of Carleton. I would also be delighted to hear my good friend and neighbour to the north, that budding politician who is making a great bid for the Liberal leadership in the province of Ontario.
I should also like to hear from the minister who represents that historic constituency within which lies what is known as the limestone city, Kingston.
Yes, I would go a little farther west to one of the other ridings I know fairly well, and in which many of my friends and acquaintances live, that of Hastings South. I would be delighted to hear the young member who represents that riding express his views on this very important issue that is before the house. I think it is a very important issue, Mr. Speaker, but I do not believe it is an urgent one. I fully realize that feelings on this issue are mixed, but the extent to which they are mixed we cannot be sure. Surely when an issue strikes at the very soul of a nation, consideration should be given in an attempt to arrive at a fundamental solution.
In my opinion, the government is off to a poor start. Should there be a plebiscite or should a committee be established? This is something to which I believe the government should give serious consideration. The proposal now before the house is mentioned in the resolution, but I am not going to take the time of the house to read it. It will never bring about, Mr. Speaker, that which the government, I hope, would wish, and that is greater unity throughout Canada. The amendment before us offers all our people some alternative. Surely, the selection of a flag is

Canadian Flag
not a one man task. Perhaps as a result of the strong feelings that exist in Canada today regarding language and culture, it is extremely difficult to unravel the threads leading to the subject of the flag, all the pros and cons of this particular issue, and to consider unemotionally and with understanding all the suggestions put forward by the various groups and organizations across this great country, all of whom desire to be known as Canadians.
A flag is described, as explained tonight by the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort-Tis-dale (Mr. Rapp), as being a piece of cloth or a device attached to a staff or halyard, used as a standard, symbol or signal. I feel certain that if Canada is to survive in the present state of confederation, such a flag must become a symbol of unity to all Canadians. Various groups hold very strong views as to what such a flag should contain by way of symbols and devices. These feelings arise from deep seated loyalties and allegiance to one or other of the founding races of Canada. The decision as to just what a national flag for Canada is to become is a very difficult one for those charged with that responsibility. While the decision will be difficult, it will also be historic and must be approached with a full realization of this position. On this decision undoubtedly will rest one of the greatest contributing factors to our country's unity or disunity for generations to come.
There are three flags prominent in the discussion concerning a flag for Canada. First there is the union jack. This flag, pure and simple, is essentially the military flag of England. It was ordained by virtue of the royal proclamation of King James in April, 1606. It is interesting to note that only 15 years later, in 1621, a flag was granted to Sir William Alexander for Nova Scotia by King James, in the charter of New Scotland. Nova Scotia is the only province of Canada to possess, through royal charter, a flag of its own, and I understand it is the pride of that province to this day. The union jack has claimed the strong allegiance of thousands of Canadians down through the years, particularly those whose ethnic origin is in the United Kingdom. In order to emphasize this point, Mr. Speaker, it is only necessary to recall the United Empire Loyalists who came to this country as pioneers to live under the union jack rather than another flag. All of those great citizens who braved the briny oceans, who came here and hewed their homes from the primeval forests, I am sure 
have left a heritage for us, of which we should all be proud.
Canada is pleased, I am sure, to regard herself as a Christian country. Most of her citizens, if not actually professing Christians at least have a certain amount of reverence for God, the Bible and all those attributes usually understood by the general term "Christianity". For this reason, the union jack has added appeal because it enshrines the upright cross which is the emblem of our Lord, yes, of our Lord's death on Calvary, for our national redemption and personal salvation.
The red ensign is described in the encyclopedia as a plain red flag bearing the union jack on the upper quarter next to the staff. This is the flag of the British merchant service and of all peoples who are not entitled to use the white or blue ensign. By the addition of a device in the fly containing the symbols of the United Kingdom, the fleur-de-lis for France and the maple leaf for Canada, this flag has been in common usage as a Canadian flag for at least two decades. It has been flown from all public buildings and government establishments in Canada. It has been used by our armed forces in various theatres of the world. It has been generally accepted by all visitors to Canada as the Canadian flag. Our men and women of the services have proudly served under the red ensign in foreign lands. To them it represented all for which they were ready and willing to lay down their lives if necessary and for it many shed their blood.
I should like to just read this poem by John McCrae. I think it is something to which every Canadian should give thought when they are thinking about wiping out the very heritage and tradition of this country, that symbol and that emblem which we have loved and cherished over the years. John McCrae wrote:
In Flanders fields the popples blow Between the crosses, row on row.
That mark our place; and in the sky The larks, still bravely singing, fly Scarce heard amid the guns below.
We are the Dead. Short days ago We lived, felt dawn, saw sunset glow,
Loved and were loved, and now we lie,
In Flanders fields.
Take up our quarrel with the foe:
To you from failing hands we throw The torch; be yours to hold it high.
If ye break faith with us who die We shall not sleep, though poppies grow In Flanders fields.
I say that we should give thought to some of those great citizens who fought and died for us. During the world wars the Canadian red ensign, the old red duster as it is called

by many, was symbolic of hope and unswerving devotion to duty on all the seven seas.
There have been strong representations, from national organizations as well as a host of individuals, that this flag be retained and confirmed as our Canadian flag. I, like other members of the house, have received many letters and suggestions for new flags, some from personal individual friends, but I would only like to put on record a couple, one being from the Smiths Falls Record-News as follows:
We felt you would be interested in being assessed the results of a readers' poll taken over the past two weeks by this newspaper. The readers were asked their preference for a national flag as well as a national anthem. The following are
the results:

Enclosed with it was an article which appeared in the newspaper and at the end of
it there was this poem:
I am ready to fight,
With all my might,
Anyone on the wrong track,
Trying to pull down our union jack.
Some say a maple leaf that's all,
To me a maple leaf turns yellow in the fall. My deepest soul Within me grieves,
Flying on a pole,
Three maple leaves.
I have another article from the same paper in which it states:
The flag debate seems to have made people and organizations conscious of our present national symbols. A number of residents of the town have started to fly their own personal flag choice from their porches and car aerials. A number of merchants have reported that they cannot keep the red ensign in stock. Latest to join the red ensign group is the Smiths Falls lawn bowling club which erected a flag pole last week.
I would also like to place on the record a letter which covers a petition signed by many hundreds of signers.
Oh, oh.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I was about to read this letter which covers a petition signed by several hundred signers:
We the undersigned feel it is about time that some voices were heard in favour of the red ensign, which a vast majority in Lanark county respect and fly as our national flag. Why a change should be proposed by Mr. Pearson to appease a small vocal group we cannot understand.
20220-460i
Canadian Flag
Mr. Pearson should be aware that his is a minority government. Only 42 per cent of the Canadian people saw fit to vote for this government, and the majority of our people decided not to do so. There has never been a prime minister since confederation who has caused so much disunity, bitterness, strife and confusion. I personally agree with some hon. members of parliament and many Canadians that Pearson is trying to ram this new flag down the throats of the Canadian people.
We, the people of Lanark county representing every religious and political affiliation along with representatives of the I.O.D.E., Orange associations, I.O.O.F., Masonic, Knights of Columbus and many others etc., etc., are opposed to any Canadian flag which does not incorporate the union jack. May we respectively solicit your support in this respect.	.
Rarely in Canadian history has a parliament presented such an unattractive picture of itself to the people who elect it, the people who pay for it. the people whose public business it is supposed to transact.
The voters are not amused, the voters are not at all impressed with what they see in Ottawa. We are disgusted and disillusioned.
We, the voters of Lanark county and petitioners go on record as being opposed to the proposed new tri maple leaf flag to replace the red ensign. Every Canadian should be granted the right to vote on this vital matter by means of a national plebiscite.
Of the many letters I have received those are all I am going to put on the record, but I would like to say a word about the proposed new flag. This flag, without any symbols of the two founding nations, is strictly Canadian design and it has been said it meets the heraldic requirements of a flag. It is not known whether this is acceptable to the French speaking population across the country, and it has been received with mixed feelings by other groups.
There are people who cannot see any good in it at all. There is another group which, though being extremely loyal to the crown of Britain, takes the view that unity in Canada is of the greatest importance, and the people in this group would accept the proposed flag in the hope that it might contribute to Canadian unity and make for a stronger Canada, which would in turn strengthen the commonwealth. In this way they feel that they would be serving the best interests of both Canada and the commonwealth. There is yet another group which subscribes to the thoughts just expressed but which hastens to add that it is in accord only with the principle of a new, distinctive Canadian flag, not with the methods being employed to bring about its approval. No individual, and no government can employ such methods without being political. I feel that a matter which so closely concerns the life of this nation should be settled in such a way as to cement the unity about which a former prime minister, Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent,

Canadian Flag
said, and I say, "Without unity, all is futile".
I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, and through you to the Prime Minister, that while the people of this bountiful land wait for important legislation to be dealt with, he, their commander in chief, obstructs the country's march to economic fulfilment by protracted debate on an issue which history records was settled years ago. The voice of Canada from sea to sea is vibrant and strong. I say to the Prime Minister: If you would have ears to hear, its voice speaks by day and by night. Can this house ignore the wishes of men and women who long since decided what flag should represent Canada on the ramparts of freedom? Is the petition presented weeks ago by the hon. members from Cumberland (Mr. Coates), York-Humber (Mr. Cowan) and Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) bearing nearly 20,000 names to be treated as a mere scrap of paper. Are not these 20,000 people who took the trouble of signing a petition to send to the parliament of Canada deserving of some consideration?
The history of this country is steeped in tradition. I trust that the Prime Minister and the members of his government will give heed to the traditions they know to be a part of this great country's inheritance. Yes, Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Prime Minister if he has closed his ears to the request of more than 250,000 gallant men and women who gave their services and offered their lives for their country, and who are now denied the right even to express their views by balloting on the flag of their choice. When the right hon. gentleman met with them in Winnipeg-I will not repeat what he said on that occasion; we have heard it several times-he as much as said: Here is your flag; take it or leave it. I think that is a pitiful experience to go down in the records of this country-that he would say this to people who fought and defended this country under the red ensign.
I fully realize we are living in a democratic country. I stand for the fullest degree of freedom and I hope we shall always have the privilege in this great land of ours to think, speak, worship and go about as we wish. But I do not think a decision of such emotional importance as this should be, or can be, decided by members of the House of Commons and still retain Canada's maximum unity. I feel that everyone who wishes to do so should have the opportunity to voice their views and opinions. The provinces [Mr. Doucett.l
which make up our dominion naturally have boundaries. But Canada is without boundaries from sea to sea and should be one Canada for all Canadians. As I say, I fully agree with the democratic process, but I feel the method employed on this occasion must be one which will keep this country united in order that we may go forward united and build on the great foundation which was so nobly laid by our forefathers.

Would the hon. member who has taken his seat permit a question? May I ask the hon. member for Lanark, my friend and neighbour, whether in view of the fact that he has made reference to the Prime Minister's address to the Royal Canadian Legion in Winnipeg he would read to this house one sentence or paragraph thereof which he regards as being evidence of poor judgment, or poor taste, or as being offensive?
The whole speech.

In reply to my hon. friend and neighbour-to use the expression he did -in case there may be some misinterpretation of the right hon. gentleman's statement I will leave it to him, when he makes his own speech, to explain in the greatest of detail what his views are. The hon. member has interrupted every speaker who has spoken in this debate-
Untrue.
And I think it is time they should have an opportunity to speak without such interruptions.

Mr. Speaker, I did not intend to take part in this debate, but in view of the slowness of the procedure and the stubbornness of some members of the house, I feel I have to take seven or eight minutes to express my constituents' views and inform the house of the feelings which have developed among the people since this debate started two weeks ago.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that the word debate no longer applies here and that what we are witnessing is much more closely connected with the world of entertainment than with parliamentary procedure.
I do not feel that the supporters of a real flag and their opponents have the right to carry on this empty discussion any longer.
More than a hundred speeches have now been delivered on the matter. Everyone has reached his own conclusions. I do not think that any argument can be added which might influence anybody.

An amendment and a subamendment have been introduced and since then speeches have been going on, most of the time outside the questions respecting this amendment asking for a referendum, or outside the subamendment which deals with the questions that might be asked in a possible plebiscite.
The Canadian people are asking more and more embarrassing questions on the nation's business.
Since when does parliament have to consult the people on such and such question after it has been sworn in? What is the role of the government? How far can the responsibility of the members of the government go? Are members of parliament so inefficient that they have to consult their electors as soon as a difficult question must be solved?
Mr. Speaker, I feel that it is high time to put an end to this sham of a debate, for the simple reason that the Canadian people are losing confidence in this wonderful institution of parliament. The Canadian people are also losing confidence in the members of this parliament, who refuse to take their responsibility and are looking for excuses to camouflage the truth.
I agree that each member should have the right to express his opinion in the house, and I respect that opinion. I also agree that the supporters of the union jack or the red ensign should defend those flags, and I recognize their merit. Were I myself in their position, I would do the same. Since they represent ridings where the electors want to maintain those symbols, they are only doing their duty and, for that reason, they deserve our respect.
But I cannot admit that responsible members of the House of Commons should hide behind this referendum smokescreen to reject the responsibility on the Canadian people.
The Canadian parliament has become the laughing stock of the people and its reputation for inefficiency is increasingly spreading, to such an extent that we are justified in wondering whether we could ever make up for all the wrong already done in this connection.
How can we claim to be qualified to administer the country and settle the serious problems of our times, if we are not even in a position to organize our own legislative program?
The deadlock where we now find ourselves is the most eloquent argument in favour of a revision of the whole procedure and I hope
Canadian Flag
that all hon. members will remember that in due time.
The Portneuf people are well known for their common sense and their innate sense of logic. Besides, they proved it in a very eloquent way during the last two elections. They are respectful of order and of our institutions, but in face of the ridiculous situation created by the discussion on the flag resolution, their faith and confidence are seriously shaken. And every time I have an opportunity to meet them, they inform me of their concern and disappointment.
Those people want a genuine Canadian flag and after the information I gave them, they still have confidence that this government will adopt such a flag. That is why I am asking the government to take all the means available to them to bring to an end, as soon as possible, this futile discussion by giving us an opportunity to express our views by voting on the matter.
I do not intend to advance any new arguments in support of the resolution or to refute certain points raised by the official opposition, because I would be afraid to fall into the same errors for which I am blaming certain of my colleagues.
The choice of the design, the timing of the introduction of the resolution, the likelihood of an eventual compromise, all those subjects have been, to my mind, sufficiently discussed. I think the institution of a committee was an elegant gesture on the part of the Prime Minister, but the terms laid down by the Leader of the Opposition were so harsh that they prove, once again, the ill will of some members.
The Prime Minister is blamed for certain withdrawals, certain retreats. It has often been said in this debate that such reversals on the part of the leader of the government are due to the fact that he is no politician. Mr. Speaker, I am glad that the Prime Minister is not a politician; unfortunately, there are too many politicians who more often than not give more thought to the next election than to the serious business of the nation.
In reaching a decision, the Prime Minister was not concerned with election results, but with a solemn promise made to the Canadian people. By his courageous action, he gained the high respect of the whole nation and, whatever may be our views on this issue, he should be commended for his courageous attitude.
The manner in which this project was presented may have been clumsy. That is

Canadian Flag
possible. However, I do not think it would be fair to discredit the whole issue because of that.
Personally, I am glad to be a member of parliament today and to participate in this historic debate. Having had the honour of supporting a truly Canadian flag will be my greatest satisfaction and probably my most pleasant memory as a member of parliament.
The Prime Minister is being criticized for his statement on a free vote. Among those who object to that, is there a single member whose vote will be affected by that statement?
Mr. Speaker, I feel that all hon. members are now sufficiently informed on the issue and that it should be put to a vote without further delay. In my opinion, the longer the final decision is delayed the greater the risk for national unity.
If, after the series of speeches that we have heard, there are still members in this house who do not feel sufficiently informed or enlightened, it will be necessary to consider amending the Elections Act to have each candidate take an I.Q. test, in addition to making a $200 deposit.
In order to maintain the reputation of parliament and its members, under the authority conferred upon parliament for the proper administration of the affairs of this country, I take the liberty to urge on the members of the government the necessity of taking action to close this debate, by extraordinary means, if need be.
Mr. Speaker, you may be sure that if I had the power to put forward a closure motion, I would be greatly pleased to do so, knowing that I would thus be doing my duty as a representative of the Canadian people.
Question.

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. We are evidently used to these noises and I was not worrying too much.
I was saying that I was interested-as are most hon. members of eastern Canada-to know what was the intention of the Minister of Forestry concerning the subsidies for the transportation of feed grains.
We learned directly from the minister and also through departmental order No. 19641155, that the government intended to establish from September 1 next new rates for the transportation of feed grains in the various parts of Quebec, Ontario, British Columbia and the maritime provinces.
Having studied the figures made available to us, I came to the conclusion that certain areas would continue to suffer discrimination while others seem to have benefited from the special attention of the minister concerned and his officials.
I refer especially to the Magdalen islands, represented by the minister, and to Newfoundland, which will both benefit from a most generous assistance for the transportation of feed grains.
I am happy, Mr. Speaker, that these areas will benefit from this assistance and I have no intention to propose a reduction of those subsidies.
On the other hand, if we compare the proposed rates, we note that $25 a ton will be granted for the transportation of grain to be delivered in Newfoundland, $7 or $9 for grain delivered in Halifax and $15 for grain delivered in the Magdalen islands. Certain factors which I find hard to assess have played a part in all that.
Mr. Speaker, with regard to the Saguenay-Lake St. John region which I have the pleasure to represent here, allow me to say that the farmers in that area will suffer from the government's new policy because starting September 1, if nothing is changed, they will have to pay 80 cents a ton more for
25, 1964	7275
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion transportation. I think that is far from what we had the right to expect and from what we had asked.
If that is the policy of farm assistance and restoration which the Minister of Forestry intends to advocate to help farming in eastern Canada, well, he has missed the boat entirely; he will have to proceed differently to restore the farm economy in our regions, particularly in the Saguenay-Lake St. John region.
Our farmers have very good land and they only need a little help in order to manage during the difficult period they are now going through.
Since we have been in the house, that is over two years ago, we have been constantly calling for some action to help farmers especially with regard to the transportation of feed grain.
After waiting so long, we finally hoped that thanks to the member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine, whom I trusted and in whom I still have some confidence, a solution would be provided.
But unfortunately, with the representatives of eastern farmers and the leaders of the Catholic farmers' union, I can only deplore this decision of the minister, and I hope that before September 1, he and his officials will acknowledge their mistakes. I hope that they will bring in some changes so that farmers of the Saguenay-Lake St. John area and others will not suffer any prejudice as a result of a mathematical error made by some officials.
We are told that it is a slight increase. Well, Mr. Speaker, in the present circumstances, the farmers are not in a position to support even a slight increase, when they had every reason and every right to expect an improvement in their situation through a reduction in the cost of feed grain which would have reduced their production cost and enabled them to compete on the markets.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the hon. gentleman for his question. I regret my inability to reply in his native tongue. I will speak slowly in order that I may communicate the thinking of the minister.
The hon. member has brought to the attention of the house the fact that farmers from the area he represents have had some problems and have expressed some complaints to the minister. The Minister of Forestry recognizes this and suggested to the hon. member

Canadian Flag
in the house today that last Friday he did receive a deputation from Quebec and, in fact, from all Canada with regard to freight assistance on feed grain. I think he would expect me to say at this particular time that under the former policy-when I say "former" I mean the policy that applied prior to the interim statement made on July 24-certain inequalities did exist. There were areas in Canada where more than freight assistance was being paid by the government and in fact this did represent a subsidy on the feed itself.
It was the hope of the minister that these inequalities might be corrected and that in addition certain assistance might apply on feed grain moved by truck in many areas. It
was hoped by the minister and by the government that the application of the assistance on feed grain moved by truck would make it more competitive and would thereby reduce the transportation costs on feed in many areas. While it is recognized that some of the subsidy may have been lost, which was over and above the freight assistance and was actually a subsidy on the feed itself, the reduction as the result of more competitive rates applying in the transportation of this feed will be a compensating factor. I think the minister expressed the thought in the house today that the views of the farmers as expressed on Friday last would be duly considered.
